The Committee is dismayed to find that even after three years of the initiation of the 12th
Plan, allocation of a mere Rs. 1.00 crore has been made for this scheme but the status of its
utilization has not been reflected. The Committee takes serious exception to the lackadaisical
approach of the Department and recommends that the Department should take corrective steps
to ensure that the scheme takes off during remaining years of the 12th Plan. (para 3.28)
G. Providing free Generic Medicines in All PH Institutions in the Country
The Committee fails to understand that a scheme of such immense importance is being
consistently allocated notional funds over the last three years of Twelfth Plan. This trend of

mark on the ability of the Department to objectively project its requirements. The Committee

105
is unable to understand as to why a huge sum of Rs. 16000 crore was earmarked for the scheme
when the Department was not prepared to implement the Scheme. The Committee impresses
upon the Department to act now with vigor and energy and see that the schemes take off at least
this year. (para 3.30)
IV. National Urban Health Mission (NUHM)-Flexible Pool
The Committee has been given to understand that under NUHM recruitment has been
made for 807 Medical Officers, 1203 Staff Nurses, 856 Pharmacists, 841 Lab Technicians, 6056
ANM against sanctioned strength of 2353, 7209, 2978, 3231 and 17584 posts, respectively. The
Committee finds that there is a wide gap between the sanctioned and the recruited manpower.
The Committee hopes that the persons recruited would actually join their respective postings.
Steps may be taken to increase allocations to the scheme and fill up all posts. (para 4.4)
V. Flexible Pool for Communicable Diseases
A. National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP)
On a perusal of the progress made in respect of the National Vector Borne Disease Control
Programme (NVBDCP), the Committee finds that for combating JE/AES, out of 181 endemic
districts, 155 districts have been covered under JE vaccination including all 60 high priority
districts of five States. The Committee is, however, of the opinion that the Department by leaving
out the remaining districts is making the fight against the diseases difficult as it is susceptible
to spread to other areas of the country. The Committee recommends that the Department should
put in place a multipronged strategy to target all identified districts at the same time to ensure
complete elimination of the disease. The Committee also recommends that the Department
should ensure vigorous efforts by means of Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
to educate the public about the precautions e.g. to have clean drinking water, etc. in order to
prevent themselves from being affected by AES. (para 5.2)
It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that dengue is claiming quite a number
of lives in the country and now the victims are losing their eye sight also due to dengue. What
is more worrisome is that dengue causing virus is mutating which is a very dangerous signal.
The Committee views this with serious concern and recommends that the matter should be
looked into seriously and urgent measures should be initiated to arrest the spread and incidence
of dengue and also to overcome the problem of mutation of dengue virus. (para 5.3)
B. National Tuberculosis (T.B) Control Programme
The Committee recommends that a mechanism may be devised by which no State falters
in submitting UCs. (para 5.6)
The Committee finds that the amount of unspent balances amounting to Rs.74.97 crore as
on 01.01.2015 does not bode well for implementation of a programme of huge scale keeping in
view the vulnerability of the population affected by this disease which has a draining effect on
not only the physical well being of the individual but also on his financial well being. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should ensure that the Centre should
encourage the States to ensure optimum utilisation of funds by means of sharing of best practices
among States. (para 5.7)

106
The Committee notes that there has been a sizeable reduction in funds allocated at RE
stage and the expenditure figures as on 5th March, 2015 leave much to be desired. The Committee
finds this extremely palpable in view of the fact that underutilization of funds can have a vital
bearing on the elimination of pathogen causing the disease. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Department should keep a tight control on effective utilization of funds to ensure that
the targeted goals are not derailed by underutilization of funds. (para 5.9)
The Committee also notes that the Department is likely to drop the DOTs programme for
treatment of TB envisaging to introduce a new therapy,  i.e. , Daily Therapy. The Committee is
of the view that in case the same is affirmative, the Department needs to have a serious
introspection on the reasons behind failure of DOTs and whether the new system of Daily
Therapy would be practicably applicable in a country of the size of India. The Committee
recommends that the Department needs to take a serious review of the DOTs programme and
also the parameters on which the Daily Therapy Programme would run keeping in view that a
change in programme would also require huge Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
efforts on the part of the Department. (para 5.10)
C. National Leprosy Control Programme
The Committee finds that there has been substantial reductions in fund allocation at RE
stage and what is more worrisome is that the Department is not even able to utilize the reduced
amount at RE stage optimally as can be seen from the utilization figures. The Committee notes
that approval has been accorded to carry out the activities in 1453 blocks in 214 districts of 19
States/UTs. The Committee while appreciating the expansion of activities would simultaneously
suggests to the Department that the expansion of the programme should not be made to suffer
due to any under-funding. Also a close monitoring of the expenditure being incurred on the
scheme is must to ensure desired results. (para 5.14)
The Committee takes note of the findings of the National Sample Survey wherein it has
been concluded that projected new cases may occur between 250,000 to 350,000 / year. The survey
has further stated that more efforts are needed for IEC, POD and DPMR activities to reduce the
deformities and to prevent progression of deformities from grade I to grade II. The Committee
is of the view that the volume of the projected new cases is a cause of serious concern and
constrained to note that inspite of adequate funds being provided at BE stage, the Department
was not able to utilize the funds for its present activities. This puts a question mark on the
smooth implementation of programme. The Committee recommends that the Department needs
to act on the findings of the Survey which reveals that more efforts are needed on the ground
for IEC, POD and DPMR activities to reduce the deformities; to prevent progression of deformities
from grade I to grade II and also keep the Committee posted of the action taken/being taken
in this regard. If required, more funds may be provided to ensure timely treatment and prevention
(para 5.16)
The Committee would like the Government to set the target of 100% Leprosy eradication
and prepare action plan in this regard. (para 5.18)
D. Integrated Disease Surveillance Project
The Committee notes that World Bank provided funds for Central Surveillance Unit (CSU)

107
in 9 States (Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu,
Uttarakhand and West Bengal) and domestic funding was made available for other States. An
allocation of Rs. 63.00 crore made in BE-2014-15 was increased to Rs.64.35 crore at RE stage.
However the expenditure figures as on 5th March, 2015 was only Rs. 48.59 crore. The Committee
is surprised that even after the allocation had been increased at RE Stage, the actual expenditure
is woefully short of even the funds allocated at BE stage. The Committee is of the opinion that
even in schemes/programmes where the funds allocation has been increased at RE stage, the
Department had miserably failed in utilizing the allocated funds and there is no justification for
increased allocation in next financial year with the trend of underutilization in the previous
years. The Committee observes that with all the where-withal of technology available at its
disposal, the Department should have made optimum utilization of funds and resources. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should prioritize activities under the
Scheme which are strictly non-negotiable and for which funds must be disbursed on priority basis
in order to ensure that the scarce budgetary resources are utilized efficiently. (para 5.22)
VI. Flexible Pool for Non-Communicable Diseases, Injury & Trauma
A. National Trachoma and Blindness Control Programme
The Committee notes that utilization status of funds in the year 2014-15 is quite satisfactory
as compared to that of the year 2013-14. The Committee is of the view that effective fund
utilization is an exercise in continuum and near utilization in one year and unsatisfactory
utilization in the previous year would not do justice to the programme and the Ministry should
ensure effective fund utilization every year, so as to preclude the Ministry of Finance from
cutting funds for the next year on the basis of the previous performance. The Committee hopes
that the Department would be able to implement the new initiatives introduced during the 12th
Plan considering that this is the fourth year of the 12th Plan. The Committee also noticed that
in both 2013-14 and 2014-15 allocations were reduced. In fact in 2013-14, it was made almost 50%
of the BE. Such drastic reductions derail the programmes and should be avoided. (para 6.3)
The Committee would like to be apprised of the action being initiated by it to check the
instance of loss of sight due to cataract surgeries in camps organized by NGO's and other
organizations. Also, the Committee through media reports came to know that only a small
percentage of eyes donated could be used for restoration of vision. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends to the Department to take adequate measures to ensure that eyes donated could
be used for the benefit of large number of blind persons and not go waste. (para 6.4)
B. National Mental Health Programme
The Committee notes that an amount of Rs. 68.28 crore was allocated for BE 2014-15 for
the National Mental Health Programme which was reduced to Rs. 62.00 crore at RE stage and
the expenditure of Rs. 58.24 crore has been incurred. The Committee, though appreciative of the
utilisation figures, is of the view that the utilisation figures vis-a-vis the funds allocated at BE
stage leave much to be desired. The Committee is of the view that Mental Health is an area of
critical importance as with the change in lifestyles and increase in stress the incidences of
depression are on the rise. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
ensure optimum utilization of funds to prevent cuts at RE stage so that the actual implementation
does not suffer due to paucity of funds. (para 6.6)

108
C. National Programme for the Health Care of Elderly (NPHCE)
The Committee is of the view that with the continuous increase in life expectancy, the
country is going to have a large Geriatric population in the near future.
The Committee finds that out of Rs. 50.83 crore allocated in BE 2014-15, the amounv has
been drastically reduced to Rs. 25.50 crore at RE stage. However, what compounds the misery,
is the utilization figure which amounts to Rs.21.47 crore. The Committee finds that the Department
has been too slow in ensuring optimum utilization of funds which would adversely affect the
actual implementation of the activities not to mention the cost overruns. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department needs to ensure that justice is done to the funds allocated by
Finance Ministry so that in future the Department should not face any cuts in allocation due to
tardy utilization record. (para 6.9)
D. National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP)
The Committee notes that the Department was allocated Rs. 40.00 crore in BE-2014-15
which has been reduced to Rs. 20.00 crore at RE stage. However the Department has been able
to spend only Rs.1.40 crore. The Committee is surprised at this state of affairs. On the one hand,
as per information of the Department, an estimated one million Indians die annually from
tobacco-related diseases, and on the other hand the Department has only been able to spend a
meagre amount of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends that such a lackadaisical
attitude cannot be condoned and such meager utilization of funds reflects on the inefficiency of
the officials manning the programme and the Department should fix the accountability to ensure
that such a situation is not allowed to recur in future. (para 6.11)
E. National Oral Health Programme (NOHP)
The Committee finds that in the year 2012-13, no allocation was made; in 2013-14, an
allocation of Rs. 10 crore was made at BE stage which was reduced to nil at RE stage and in 2014-
15 an allocation of Rs. 2.66 crore was made at BE stage which was reduced to Rs 2.00 crore at
RE stage and the actual expenditure was to the tune of Rs 1.68 crore. Further a mere allocation
of Rs. 2.00 crore has been made in 2015-16. The Committee is dismayed to find that even after
three years of the inception of the programme the allocation and utilization figures leave much
to be desired keeping in view that a plan outlay of Rs. 100 crore was made for the entire Plan
period. The Committee feels that keeping in view that only 2 more years of 12th Plan are left,
it would be a herculean task to ensure achieving the target set for the 12th Plan. The Committee
points out that the Department had not been able to initiate the programme in the 11th Plan
and the progress in the 12th Plan is not satisfactory at all. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Department should prioritise the schemes on which it can ensure deliverables instead
of stretching itself thin on introducing schemes and then being not able to deliver the same, of
which this programme is a classic case. (para 6.14)
F. Assistance to States for Capacity Building
The Committee finds that an amount of Rs.4.17 crore was allocated in the 2014-15 at BE
stage, but the same was reduced to nil allocation at RE stage. The Committee fails to understand
how the Department is proposing to implement the scheme when no allocations has been made
at RE stage. What is more appalling is the non-receipt of the utilization figures by the Department.

109
The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to complete the targets set for the 12th
Plan period and also recommends the Department to be more circumspect in ensuring utilization
of funds more so in view of the fact that an allocation of Rs. 20.00 crore has been made in 2015-
16. (para 6.16)
G. National Programme for Prevension and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease
and Stroke
The Committee notes that an amount of Rs. 292.55 crore was allocated in 2014-15 at BE
stage which was reduced to Rs. 235.00 crore at RE stage and the actual expenditure is Rs.190.34
crore. The Committee observes that the country has been witnessing a rapid increase in the
cases of cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and stroke which are affecting people from all
strata of the society. The Committee would, therefore, like the Department to take more
intensive and dispersed initiatives to ensure preventing the incidence of these cases. The Committee
also notes that the utilisation figures, when compared to the BE and RE allocations, do not do
justice to the Programme and recommends that the Department should ensure that the scheme
is prioritised as 'essential' on which no compromise can be allowed and the Committee feels that
nil allocation to the Programme in 2015-16 is not digestable and the Department should approach
the Ministry of Finance for allocation of funds at RE stage. (para 6.19)
VII. Miscellaneous Issues
Provision of Hearing Aids, Spectacles, Dentures etc. to the Senior Citizens in Rural Areas under
NRHM
It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that the National Rural Health Mission
in the country which is mandated to provide health care in rural India focuses mainly on
treatment of diseases. There is no provision to provide spectacles, dentures and hearing aids etc.
particularly to senior citizens in the rural areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department should look at the feasibility of the proposal for providing the aids and appliances
mentioned above to the senior citizens in the rural areas under NRHM and, accordingly allocate
adequate the funds for the purpose. (para 7.1)

110
PART C
NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL ORGANISATION
I. Introduction
The Committee notes that there is a declining trend of people living with HIV/AIDS in the
country according to HIV Sentinel Surveillance (HSS). The Committee though appreciates the
efforts made by NACO for bringing a steady decline in HIV prevalence in the country but would
also like to know whether the mechanism put in a place to count the people living with HIV/
AIDS is robust and reflects the exact count. (para 1.4)
III. Budgetary Allocation
The Committee notes that as compared to the funds allotted in REs 2012-13, 2013-14 and
2014-15, the level of utilization of funds by NACO has been satisfactory, though it is less than
the allocations made in BEs of the respective years. A perusal of the information made available
to the Committee, revealed that according to HIV Sentinel Surveillance 2012-13, which is mandated
to assess the burden and trends of HIV in different States of the country, the overall HIV
prevalence among the general population continues to be low at 0.35% in the country, with an
overall declining trend at the national level. The estimated number of People Living with HIV/
AIDS has also maintained a steady declining trend from 23.2 lakh in 2006 to 20.9 lakh in 2011.
The Committee feels that this is due to the impact of the various interventions of NACP and
scaled up prevention strategies. But what is worrisome is that some low prevalence States like
Assam, Chandigarh, Delhi, Jharkhand etc. have shown increase in the number of new infections.
In this context the Committee is concerned about the reduced allocation for NACO for 2015-16.
The Committee feels that the allocation of Rs.1397.00 crore in RE 2015-16 which is only marginally
higher than the RE 2014-15 allocation of Rs.1300.00 crore may have and adverse impact on the
key priorities of National AIDS Control Programme IV and hinder scale-up of interventions in
hitherto untouched areas. The Committee sincerely hopes that subsequent to the increase of
State share in the Central Taxes from 32 per cent to 42 per cent, the State Governments, who
are currently not contributing any money to National AIDS Control Programme (NACP), would
be able to fund a proportion of the fund requirement from their State Health Budgets. The
Committee, simultaneously, observes that India is a resource-constrained country and in order
to obtain the best possible health outcomes, it is imperative that allocation of resources is
prioritized across competing ends and the available funds are deployed in a more efficient
manner. The Committee, therefore, recommends that concrete steps should be initiated to
economize on expenditure and improve its efficiency so that the intended objectives of NACP IV
are not adversely impacted. (para 3.5)
IV. Unspent Cash Balances with State AIDS Control Society (SACS)
The Committee notes that inspite of interventions of NACO, availability of unspent balances
with some SACS are still quite high. The Committee, therefore, recommends the NACO to
introduce stricter monitoring mechanism and plan viable strategy to clear the unspent balances
so that funds do not get accumulated and locked but are utilized in a more productive manner.
The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 70th Report on Demands
for Grants 2013-14 of the erstwhile Department of AIDS Control that in order to ensure timely
110

111
and effective utilization of unspent balances, NACO should insist on quarterly feedback from all
the SACS. The Committee also desires to be apprised of the number and dates of review
meetings taken in 2014-15 to expedite liquidation of the unspent cash balances with SACS.
(para 4.3)
V. Role of NGOs
The Committee welcomes the action initiated by NACO to deal with the issues - like
recovery of unspent balances with discontinued NGOs and steps taken for monitoring and control
of programmatic and financial activities etc. The Committee, would, however, like the Department
to make an assessment of the impact of actions initiated for a recovery of unspent balances with
defaulting NGO's. (para 5.3)
VI. Metro Blood Banks
The Committee notes that the proposal for setting up of Metro Blood Banks is one of the
approved activities under NACP-III and has been continued in NACP-IV . But its implementation
is still a far cry. Budgetary allocations to the tune of Rs. 83.00 crore was made in BE 2014-15
but was surrendered in toto due to pending approval of Expenditure Finance Committee. The
Committee disapproves of providing as much as Rs. 83.00 crore in BE 2014-15 although necessary
approval of EFC remained to be obtained for implementing the project and exhorts that maximum
possible care be taken while formulating Budget Estimates under this head in future so that
realistic projection of funds requirements is ensured. Now that the project has been approved,
the Committee recommends the Department to ensure that this important project is taken up
for implementation without further delay. The Committee would like to be updated on the
progress made towards implementation of this project and targeted time line for its completion.
(para 6.3)
VII. Setting up of New District Level Blood Banks
The Committee notes that the NACP-III was to be implemented during 2007-2012. The
Committee finds that out of the 39 new District Level Blood Banks to be set up during NACP-
III, 8 DLLB are still to be implemented even though three years have elapsed since NACP-III
concluded. The Committee notes that most of the reasons cited for the delay are non-availability
of necessary infrastructure, manpower and delay in issuance of license. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Department to play a pro-active role by taking up the matter with the concerned
State Governments as well as its agencies at an appropriate level to iron out the procedural
hindrances and help achieve the targets set. The Committee also gathers that equipment for the
Centres were procured and supplied during NACP-Il. The Committee is perturbed to find such
a national waste in resource country like ours. (para 7.3)
On enquiring about the position of special care of the underserved areas including districts
of Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand in respect of blood banks, the NACO has informed
that communications have been sent to all States to make blood storage centres functional with
support from NHM to improve access to safe blood for underserved areas. The Committee would
like to be apprised about the progress made in this regard. (para 7.4)
VIII. Antiretoviral Therapy (ART) Centre
The Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in respect of setting up of
134 ART centres which are proposed to be made functional by March, 2017, within a period of
six months from the date of presentation of this Report. (para 8.3)

112
IX. Setting up of Plasma Fractionation Centre (PFC)
The Committee desires that the project should take off at the earliest. All necessary steps
may be taken in this direction. (para 9.3)
X. Setting up of District AIDS Prevention and Control Units (DAPCUs)
The Committee appreciates the efforts of NACO to set up 189 DAPCUs in the country. The
Committee notes that further expansion of DAPCUs would be undertaken, if required, after
finalization of district re-categorization which is still in process. The Committee recommends
that the district re-categorization should be completed at the earliest. (para 10.2)

REPORT
I. Introduction
1.1 The Department of Health Research (DHR) was created as a separate Department within the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by an amendment to the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961 on the 17th September 2007. The Department became functional from November
2008 with the appointment of first Secretary of the Department.
1.2 The aim of the DHR/ICMR is to bring modern health technologies to the people through research
and innovations related to diagnosis, treatment methods and vaccines for prevention; to translate them
into products and processes and, in synergy with concerned organizations introduce these innovations
into public health system.
The following 10 functions (nine new functions, plus the ongoing function of administering the ICMR)
have been allocated to the Department of Health Research:
1. Promotion and co-ordination of basic, applied and clinical research including clinical trials
and operational research in areas related to medical, health, biomedical and medical profession
and education through development of infrastructure, manpower and skills in cutting edge
areas and management of related information thereto.
2. Promote and provide guidance on research governance issues, including ethical issues in
medical and health research.
3. Inter-sectoral coordination and promotion of public - private - partnership in medical,
biomedical and health research related areas.
4. Advance training in research areas concerning medicine and health, including grant of
fellowships for such training in India and abroad.
5. International co-coperation in medical and health research, including work related to
international conferences in related areas in India and abroad.
6. Technical support for dealing with epidemics and natural calamities.
7. Investigation of outbreaks due to new and exotic agents and development of tools for
prevention.
8. Matters relating to scientific societies and associations, charitable and religious endowments
in medicine and health research areas.
9. Coordination between organizations and institutes under the Central and State Governments
in areas related to the subjects entrusted to the Department and for the promotion of special
studies in medicine and health.
10. Administering and monitoring of Indian Council of Medical Research.
1.3 With a view to fulfill its mandate of nine new functions, the DHR had formulated following five
new schemes and all these schemes have since been approved and rolled out in 2013-14.
(i) Establishment of Multidisciplinary Research Units (MRUs) in Govt. Medical Colleges and
Research Institute.

2
(ii) Establishment of Model Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs) in the States.
(iii) Establishment of Network of Research Laboratories for Managing Epidemics and Natural
Calamities.
(iv) Human Resource Development for Health Research.
(v) Grants in Aid Scheme for inter-sectoral convergence & promotion and guidance on research
governance issues.
1.4 The Department has also been working on bringing suitable legislations aimed at:
(i) Regulating ethical issues pertaining to biomedical and heath research;
(ii) Regulating medical, social, ethical and legal aspects of surrogacy; and
(iii) Assisted reproductive technology services in the country, and also for regulating the processes
for recognition of any proposed alternative systems of medicine.

2.6 As evident from the above tables there are huge variations between the BE and RE for all
the schemes as well as for ICMR. The reasons cited by the Department for this trend were non-
receipt of adequate number of applications on account of approval of the scheme at fag end of

non-completion of requisite administrative and technical formalities under the Schemes guidelines
by certain States. The Committee, in the circumstances, is constrained to observe that inspite
of its repeated recommendations to the Department to take all out measures, including completion
of pre-project planning and formalities of obtaining necessary approvals for optimum and judicious
utilization of budgeted funds, not much has been done in this regard. The Committee fails to
understand the reasons for the delay in formulation of all the schemes even though the Schemes
first got in- principle approval by the Planning Commission in December 2010. The Committee
is not convinced with the statement of the Department that inspite of its best efforts, the various
actions like the appraisal of the Schemes, responding to various appraisal agencies, clearance of
the Schemes by EFC/CCEA took more than anticipated time which ultimately led to the delay.
The Committee observes that this is a clear case of lack of foresight and faulty planning by the
Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make all
possible efforts with proper and timely planning to utilize the allocated funds at BE Stage. The
Committee would like to be apprised of the steps being taken or proposed to be taken to arrest
this trend of underutilization of budgeted funds which eventually led to massive cuts at RE stage.

(b) It would not be possible to sanction new Units/Labs as per the EFC approved targets in

and Guidance on Health Research of Public Health importance: (ii) Human Resource
Development for Health Research will be adversely affected.

(i) Priority will be given to release the 2nd installment in respect of already sanctioned
Units/Labs under MRU, MRHRU and VRDL, instead of sanctioning the new ones till
adequate budgetary allocations are made available.
(ii) The Research programmes will be limited to funds available under GIA schemes and
with limited funds HRD programme will also be limited to funds available. All the
funds released in 2013-14 and 2014-15 have been fully utilized.
2.10 As regards the ICMR it has been informed that the following activities are likely to be affected
due to the short fall of budget:
(a) Nine major SFC/EFC ongoing proposals for providing civil infrastructure, equipment and
machineries in ICMR for promoting biomedical and health research will be affected.
(b) Seven New SFC/EFC proposals for providing civil infrastructure, equipment and machineries
in ICMR for promoting biomedical and health research will be affected.
(c) About 500 new Adhoc research programmes initiated and about 2500 ongoing research
programmes including 11 projects on tribal health will also be affected.
It has been informed that ICMR proposes to offset the effect of shortfall by funding only ongoing
priority items and funding for all new research programmes will be limited to funds available.

2.11 The Committee is of the opinion that keeping in view the mandate of DHR/ICMR to bring
modern technologies to the people through research and innovations and the fact that Department
has just launched the above mentioned Schemes to fulfill its mandate of creating a strong and
effective eco-system for carrying out health research in the country and for introduction of new
technologies, new methods of treatment and products/ processes into the public health system;
any under funding to the schemes would prove detrimental in achieving the desired objectives
that too at a time when these schemes have just picked up their pace. In view of the fact that
with this funds crunch it would not be possible for the Department to roll out many of its
proposed initiatives under the schemes, the Committee recommends that the Department should
vigorously pursue with the Ministry of Finance for enhanced funds at RE Stage. The Committee,
simultaneously, also recommends to the Department that it should take all out efforts for
optimum and judicious utilization of available resources and funds for implementation of various
Schemes. Funds for new initiatives should be limited to availability of funds.
III. Indian Council of Medical Research. (ICMR)
3.1 As per the information given in the Annual Report of the Department, ICMR serves as the fulcrum
of the Department of Health Research. It is an apex organization to formulate, conduct and promote
biomedical research. It has been mentioned that the proposed seamless integration between the ICMR
(generation of new knowledge) and the DHR (putting this knowledge to public good) which began in
recent past has been progressing well in the right direction.
3.2 ICMR carries out intramural research through its institutes/centres. Of 32 institutes/centres, 17
deal with communicable diseases and coordinated by Division of Epidemiology and Communicable
Diseases; 7 with non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and are coordinated by Division of RCH; 3 deal
with diseases related to nutrition and are coordinated by Division of Nutrition and 3 deal with diseases
related to basic medical sciences (BMS) and are coordinated by Division of BMS.
3.3 Besides, ICMR funds extramural research in medical Colleges, Universities/Institutions. An average
of 1200-1500 projects annually are funded which include both ongoing and new projects. ICMR provides
1200-1500 students fellowships - JRF, SRF, PDF, STS ongoing and new, every year.

of expenditure of Rs. 179.36 crore upto 4.3.2015 could be made against the allocations of Rs.
5213.00 crore made for the Schemes for 12th Plan Period. The Committee understands that all
the Schemes could be rolled in the year 2013-14 only and hence the expenditure booked was very
low. The Committee, however, is constrained to comment that this state of affairs indicates that
the Department was consistently over estimating its requirements and has not been able to make
use of scarce financial resources. The Committee, accordingly, impresses upon the Department
to make all out efforts to implement its proposed activities under the schemes in the remaining
two years of the 12th Five Year Plan for optimum utilization of allocations and for achieving the
desired objectives. (para 2.3)
As evident from the above tables there are huge variations between the BE and RE for all
the schemes as well as for ICMR. The reasons cited by the Department for this trend were non-
receipt of adequate number of applications on account of approval of the scheme at fag end of
2013-14, pendency of utilization certificates, receipt of less number of proposals from States and
non-completion of requisite administrative and technical formalities under the Schemes guidelines
by certain States. The Committee, in the circumstances, is constrained to observe that inspite
of its repeated recommendations to the Department to take all out measures, including completion
of pre-project planning and formalities of obtaining necessary approvals for optimum and judicious
utilization of budgeted funds, not much has been done in this regard. The Committee fails to
understand the reasons for the delay in formulation of all the schemes even though the Schemes
first got in- principle approval by the Planning Commission in December 2010. The Committee
is not convinced with the statement of the Department that inspite of its best efforts, the various
actions like the appraisal of the Schemes, responding to various appraisal agencies, clearance of
the Schemes by EFC/CCEA took more than anticipated time which ultimately led to the delay.
The Committee observes that this is a clear case of lack of foresight and faulty planning by the
Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make all
possible efforts with proper and timely planning to utilize the allocated funds at BE Stage. The
Committee would iike to be apprised of the steps being taken or proposed to be taken to arrest
this trend of underutilization of budgeted funds which eventually led to massive cuts at RE stage.
(para 2.6)
The Committee is of the opinion that keeping in view the mandate of DHR/ICMR to bring
modern technologies to the people through research and innovations and the fact that Department
has just launched the above mentioned Schemes to fulfill its mandate of creating a strong and
effective eco-system for carrying out health research in the country and for introduction of new
technologies, new methods of treatment and products/ processes into the public health system;
any under funding to the schemes would prove detrimental in achieving the desired objectives
that too at a time when these schemes have just picked up their pace. In view of the fact that
with this funds crunch it would not be possible for the Department to roll out many of its
proposed initiatives under the schemes, the Committee recommends that the Department should
19

20
vigorously pursue with the Ministry of Finance for enhanced funds at RE Stage. The Committee,
simultaneously, also recommends to the Department that it should take all out efforts for
optimum and judicious utilization of available resources and funds for implementation of various
Schemes. Funds for new initiatives should be limited to availability of funds. (para 2.11)
III. Indian Council of Medical Research. (ICMR)
The Committee puts on record its appreciation for ICMR for near optimum utilization of
allocated funds. Such a trend of utilization by the Institute would strengthen its demand for
additional funds at RE stage during the current year, as per the projections made. However, the
Committee would also like to say that mere utilization of funds is not an indicator of success,
unless the research outcomes are translated into health products or are used in better interest
of people. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps being taken in speedy translation
of research leads into public utilities. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the
number of leads which were actually put into public use for their betterment. (para 3.6)
The Committee is happy to note that at its behest the Department has revisited its
priorities areas for research and drawn three most important priorities areas namely Cancer
Research, Environmental Health and Maternal and Child Health for carrying out research. The
Committee is hopeful that this move of the Department would result in visible and desirable
results. The Committee desires to be apprised of the outcome of the above move.   (para 3.11)
The Committee appreciates the intervention made by the Department in the area of
environmental pollution and desires that research activities should not be restricted to air
pollution only as the health hazards of water/noise pollution are also affecting a large chunk of
population. (para 3.18)
During the presentation on ICMR, the Committee was apprised about the network of
ICMR Institutes/Centres spread across the country. On a perusal thereof, the Committee noted
that there are regional imbalances in the presence of ICMR across the country. The Committee
noted that a large area of the Central India which also happened to be tribal area which is
malaria infected and affected with various other environment- related morbidity factors is not
covered under the projects on traditional medicines. The Committee, accordingly, recommends
to the Department to pay attention to those areas which are not well served and seek additional
resources for Eastern India and Central India. (para 3.20)
IV. Programmes for the North East (NE)
(B) ICMR: From a perusal of the initiatives proposed for NE region in the year 2015-16
vis-a-vis those taken in the year 2014-15, the Committee notes that nothing new region specific
programme has been envisaged for the current year. The actual expenditure incurred vis-a-vis
allocations made in the year 2014-15 is also not very promising and reflects that many of the
proposed initiatives visualized for the year perhaps were either delayed or not accomplished. The
Committee hence exhorts that the Department may take all measures for optimum and judicious
utilization of the allocations made in the current financial year for the NE region. (para 4.3)
V. Human Resource Development for Health Research:
The Committee fails to understand as to why there was so much delay in implementing
the scheme which resulted in surrender of the entire budgeted funds for the year 2012-13 and
drastic reduction of allocations in RE 2013-14. Trained and qualified manpower is pre-requisite
for implementation of various research schemes of the Department. The Committee, therefore,

21
recommends that the Department must complete all pre-project activities timely and properly to
avoid recurrence of the existing trend of underutilization. Allocation may be increased at RE
stage, if necessary, depending on the number of eligible proposals received. Publicity may be
given to the Scheme. (para 5.6)
VI. Development of Infrastructure for Promotion of Health Research
(i) Establishment of Multi-disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) in Govt. Medical Colleges
and the Research Institutes.
The Committee observes that deaths caused due to non-communicable diseases are much
more than those occurring due to communicable diseases and any under-funding to the Scheme,
which promotes research in Non-Communicable diseases, will prove detrimental to control lifestyle
diseases. The proposed shortfall in allocation to the Scheme may lead to curtailment in the
second or subsequent installments to the Institutes where the Department has already made a
beginning and would result in seriously hampering of research activities initiated. The Committee,
therefore, lends its support to the demand of the Department for enhancement of allocations at
RE Stage for the Scheme so that investments already made in the medical colleges under the
Scheme do not go down the drain.
The Committee finds that life style-related disease like hypertension, blood pressure,
diabetes etc. are on the rise and are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the country
and, therefore, it is a cause of serious concern. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
life style-related diseases may be included in the research programmes of the Department.
(para 6.6)
(ii) Establishment of Model Rural Health Units (MRHRUs)
The Committee desires that more States may be covered under the Scheme. The Department
may also set up more MRHRUs covering all the States. (para 6.10)
VII. Grant-in-aid for Inter sectoral Convergence and Promotion and guidance on Health
Research:
The Committee observes that some of very important activities are targeted to be
accomplished under the Scheme for Inter Sectoral convergence and Promotion and Guidance on
Health Research. The Committee is happy to note that pursuant to its recommendation made
in 56th Report and reiterated in 67th Report for creation of an institutional co-ordination
mechanism for synergizing the core competencies of the different organizations/agencies a group
of Secretaries has been constituted, consisting of Secretaries from DBT, DRDO, DARE/ICAR,
ISRO, Department of Space, DIT etc. to co-ordinate and collaborate on Health Research activities
among various departments. The Committee hopes that anticipated dividends are being accrued
from this move. (para 7.8)
The Committee apprehends that shortfall in allocations made for the Scheme would hamper
the pace of projects already initiated. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department
to take all measures to offset impact of shortfall of allocations. Simultaneously, the Department
should also present a strong case for seeking more funds at RE Stage. (para 7.9)
VIII. Establishment of Network of Laboratories of managing Epidemics and Natural Calamities:
The Committee fails to see through the reasons for underperformance under the Scheme
of Establishment of Network of Laboratories of managing Epidemics and Natural Calamities.

22
With this pace of performance, the Committee does not understand how the target of establishing
10 Regional Labs, 30 State Level Labs and 120 Medical Colleges Labs, as envisaged during the
12th Plan period would be achieved. Even funds could be released to only 4 Regional Labs, 5 State
Level Labs and 16 Medical Colleges Labs out of the approved 5 Regional Labs, 11 State Level
Labs and 35 Medical College Labs. The Department needs to do some serious introspection to
look into the cause for not meeting the targets set. The Committee impresses upon the Department
to draw an action plan to meet the physical and financial targets set under the Scheme.
(para 8.7)
The Committee is perturbed to find that the component for creation of the Revolving fund
to facilitate a rapid mobilization of outbreak/ disaster response to infectious diseases outbreak
or a natural or man made disaster was not approved in the EFC meeting held under the
Chairmanship of Finance Secretary and Secretary of Expenditure. The Committee observes that
creation of such a fund was very vital for the country owing to recent outbreaks of diseases like
Swine Flu, Chikunguniya etc. As the Department has also expressed its inability to establish a
budget line to cater for the emergency action in case of infectious diseases outbreak, the
Committee recommends that the Department may approach the Ministry of Finance for reviewing
its decision in the matter. (para 8.8)

REPORT
Introduction
1. The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) was established as a
separate Department under Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India in 1995. It was
renamed as Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) in
November, 2003. The Department of AYUSH has now been made an independent Ministry w.e.f. 09.11.2014.
The Ministry is mandated for policy, planning and program implementation for growth, development and
propagation of AYUSH systems across national and international fronts. Sowa Rigpa is the recent inclusion
to the family of AYUSH systems. The Ministry under its purview has National Institutes, Research Councils,
Regulatory Bodies, Pharmacopoieal Laboratories, Pharmacopoeia Commission, medicines manufacturing
enterprise and National Medicinal Plants Board.
2. The Twelfth Five Year Plan aims at promoting the health goals with appropriate utilization of AYUSH
in the health delivery system based on their strength areas and interventions for health promotion and
management of disease burden.
3. All the existing Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) have been merged into a single umbrella Scheme
namely, National AYUSH Mission (NAM) and introduced w.e.f. 29.09.2014.
4. The scope of Pharmacopoeia Commission of Indian Medicine was expanded to include Homoeopathy
in its purview with necessary fundamental changes in the structure for smooth performance.
5. Approval of National AYUSH Mission, as a unified Centrally Sponsored Scheme, will help to support
implementation of state programs and projects with more flexibility and better funding pattern. Revised
Central Schemes for public health interventions of AYUSH, Extra Mural Research, Development of Industry
Clusters, promotional activities of AYUSH, International co-operation and incentive to the industry are meant
for propelling propagation of AYUSH in tandem with the public aspirations and needs.
6. The proposed budget amounting to Rs.1008 crore for the financial year 2015-16 would be utilized for
comprehensive development of AYUSH sector. Further, the outcomes would go a long way in giving much
needed boost towards providing health care services and global leadership of the country in the field of
traditional medicine.
7. The Ministry under its purview has two Regulatory Councils, five Research Councils, seven National
Institutes, two Pharmacopeia Laboratories, a National Medicinal Plants Board and a public sector undertaking
for manufacture of Ayurveda & Unani medicine.
8. During the Twelfth Plan period, the Ministry seeks to strengthen initiatives taken earlier to expand the
reach of health care through Traditional Systems of Medicine. The Twelfth Plan duly recognized the fact
that the strengths of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, if suitably used, can help advance the
goals of the Twelfth Plan. AYUSH systems would be main-streamed using their areas of strengths namely in
preventive and promotive health care, diseases and health conditions relating to women and children, older
persons, Non-communicable diseases, preventive health care, mental ailments, stress management, palliative
care, rehabilitation and health promotion.

16. Explaining the persistent under-utilization of allocated funds over the years, the Secretary (AYUSH)
during his evidence before the Committee on 31st March, 2015, attributed the main reasons for less utilization
of funds to structural weaknesses of State AYUSH Institutions, less absorption capacity of the States and

17. The Secretary also enumerated the following steps taken to ensure that the un-utilized balance is
minimized.
(i) The Ministry has comprehensively reviewed the expenditure profile of each major scheme/
programme before preparing the budget estimates.
(ii) Timely release and assimilation of funds by State Governments/ Institutes/Councils and other
organizations, is being emphasized.
(iii) Nodal Officers for individual States have been nominated by Ministry of AYUSH to follow-up
the matter with individual States for liquidation of outstanding UCs.
(iv) Regular meetings with state officials are held at the level of Secretary (AYUSH) to emphasize
and ensure optimal and efficient utilization of funds. In the first-ever meeting of state AYUSH
Ministers Chaired by Hon'ble Minister (IC), AYUSH the issue of pending Utilization Certificates
has also been reviewed.
(v) Scheme-wise Roadmaps for future utilisation of funds have been drawn for efficient and
timely utilization of funds - particularly in the first and second quarter of the next financial year
and identify possible bottlenecks well in advance and address the same. For example, emphasis
is laid on holding of the regular meetings of Mission Directorate, Project Screening Committee
(PSC), Technical Screening Committee (TSC) and Standing Finance Committee (SFC) etc.
for various schemes, well in advance so as to ensure timely release of funds in 2015-16.
(vi) One of the flagship schemes, the National AYUSH Mission (NAM), was approved and notified
on 29.09.2014. NAM focuses on implementation efficiency and improving absorption capacity
of the States through setting up of State AYUSH Societies and strengthening of State Programme
Management Units with adequate staff and infrastructure for implementing and monitoring the
mission activities. One of the criteria for deciding the allocation 'envelop' to the states is their
track record in utilizing funds in the past.
(vii) Action plan from 27 States for Rs. 185.72 already sanctioned. The required budget Head for
NAM has already been created. Out of Rs. 185.72 crore merely Rs. 9.90 crore could be
released so far. Around Rs.120 crore is estimated to be released for already approved NAM
action plans in the first quarter of the next year itself against a total annual allocation of Rs.318
crore.
(viii) The Ministry is also working to support the States to strengthen the institutional framework
and improve capacity for better leverage and efficacy in utilization of funds. For example,

7
under NAM, there is a specific component for strengthening State Programme Management
Units. The 21 States/ UTs have already intimated the constitutions of State AYUSH Societies
and other states/ UTs are also gearing up for the constitution of AYUSH Societies. Similarly
support to State Medicinal Plant Boards has been significantly increased under the revised
Central Sector Scheme Guidelines of the NMPB.
18. The Secretary also drew attention of the Committee to the changeover from the Society route of
funds to the Treasury Route in the financial year 2014-15. He stated that earlier the funds were released to
the State Health Societies directly. As per the new arrangement, funds have to go to the State Budgets. The
State Governments have to contribute their share and draw that amount and pass it on to the Health societies.
The Secretary submitted that in the direct transmission of money from the Central Government to the State
Health Society through the Treasury Route, UC conditionality is not an absolute bar for release of funds. He
also submitted that the problems have now been largely ironed out and utilization rate of funds is expected
to increase in the financial year 2015-16 because all the Centrally Sponsored Schemes are to be funded
through the Treasury Route. Highlighting the weak AYUSH structures in the States, the Secretary informed
the Committee that in the entire country only two States, namely Uttarakhand and Rajasthan have separate

22. The Committee is concerned to find that there were savings of significant magnitude under
several important heads during 2013-14 and 2014-15 as is evident from Table Nos. 2 and 3 given
above. The fact that the savings were not just the result of implementation of economy measures
but occurred due to various reasons like non-filing of posts, non-approval of schemes, delay in
execution work, slow space of construction etc, clearly suggests that there were inadequacies in the
monitoring mechanism, as well as budgetary planning process and budget allocations were proposed
without obtaining all necessary clearances. The Committee is of the firm view that the savings
would have been minimized substantially if proper internal auditing and streamlined monitoring
mechanisms had been in place and periodic review of the trends and progress of expenditure had
been adopted. The Committee notes that the Ministry of AYUSH has initiated, at the behest of this
Committee, a number of steps to ensure optimal and efficient utilization of allotted funds. The
Committee would like the Ministry to scrupulously implement the initiatives taken in this regard
and simultaneously evaluate the impact of new initiatives on utilization of budgeted funds. The
Committee would like to be kept apprised of the impact of the new initiatives taken on utilization
of budgeted funds.
23. The Committee is constrained to note that there has been persistent and substantial
underutilization of Plan funds under the heads - "Hospitals and Dispensaries", "Educational
Institutions", "Research and Development including Medicinal Plants", "Development of AYUSH
Industry", and "National Mission on AYUSH". The allocations made in BE 2013-14 and BE 2014-15
under the above heads, were subsequently revised downwards at the RE stage and the sums which
remained grossly underutilized, were surrendered by the end of the year. The Committee observes
that such huge variations in BE, RE and Actuals are indicative of the fact that principles of fiscal
prudence and discipline were neither observed nor proper assessment of the projects was carried
out. The Committee observes that in a resource-constrained country like India, all care needs to be
taken to ensure that the scarce resources do not remain locked up and surrendered at the fiscal
end. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry chalk out its fiscal roadmap in such
a way that the allocated funds are utilized optimally and more productively under the above Heads
and such a situation does not recur in future.
24. From a scrutiny of information furnished, it is revealed that the entire budgeted plan funds
had to be surrendered due to non-approval of certain Schemes. For example, a sum of Rs. 4.00 crore
and Rs. 25.00 crore had been proposed in BE 2013-14 and BE 2014-15 respectively under the head
"All India Institute of Unani Medicine." The Ministry spent a meagre Rs. 0.20 crore in 2013-14
while the entire budgeted funds for 2014-15 had to be surrendered due to non-approval of the
project. What is alarming is that this is not the only example of surrender of the entire budgeted
funds. Similar is the case with quite a few other projects such as "All India Institute of Yoga", "All
India Institute of Homoeopathy", "Homoeopathic Medicines Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd",
"Pharmacovigilance Initiative for ASU drugs", "National Institute of Medicinal Plants", etc. The
Committee deprecates the Ministry for making unrealistic projection of fund requirements without
obtaining necessary approvals for implementation of the above projects. The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that the Ministry should ensure that all pre-approval formalities are completed
before budget allocations are proposed and realistic financial outlays are earmarked for the above
projects/schemes. There is no point in making ritualistic allocations which remain on paper only.
25. The Committee observes that to obtain greater evenness in the budgeted expenditure within

Updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy
47. The updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy has been engaging the attention
of the Committee for quite some time. In reply to a question regarding the status of updation of Central
Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy, the Ministry has furnished the following information
(Annexure - 1). On being asked about the time lag between the receipt of information from the State
Governments and its updation into the Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy, the Ministry
have furnished the following information:
"As regards time lag of updation in the Central Registers of Indian Medicine, it is informed that the procedure
for entry of information received from the State Boards/Councils to Central Register takes at least four to six
months depending on the number of practitioners registered in the State Register because the procedure
includes, inter alia, that:
(i) State Register is screened keeping in view that all the particulars fulfilling the requirement of
the CCIM of the registered practitioners are furnished in respective columns;
(ii) Further screening of the State Register is done to ensure that the practitioners are possessing
recognized medical qualification of Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha included in the Schedules to
IMCC Act, 1970;
(iii) Translation of Central Register of Indian Medicine from English to Hindi or vice versa;
(iv) Thereafter the Central Register is typed bilingually in English and Hindi and compared to the
State Register in order to ensure the correctness of the same; and
(v) The prepared Central Register in English and Hindi is sent/submitted to the Controller of
Publication, Deptt. of Publication, Govt, of India for its Gazette Notification in the Gazette of
India.
48. Regarding time lag of updation in the Central Registers of Homoeopathy, it is informed that the state
Registers, as and when received, are scrutinized and'as required, clarifications are sought by C.C.H. from
State Boards/ Councils which require some time. However, on an average taking data from State Register to
Central Register consumes three months to 24 months in view of the said reason."
49. The Committee regrets to note that despite its earlier recommendation to timely update the
Central Registers of the Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, not much headway has
been made in the matter, mainly due to delay in submission of accurate information by the State
Boards and its incorporation in the Central Registers. This is contrary to a provision in the Indian
Medicine Central Council (IMCC) Act 1970 which mandates the State Boards to submit updated
registers of practitioners on the first of April every year. The Committee is also dismayed to note
from the information furnished that the data received from the States is often found to have several
inaccuracies which further delays the updation of the Registers. The Committee is also surprised to
note that the time-lag between the receipt of information from the State Governments and its
updation /incorporation is 6 to 9 months in respect of the Central Register of Indian Medicine and
3 to 24 months in respect of the Central Register of Homoeopathy. Given the IT resources currently
available, the Committee is unable to reconcile itself with this huge time-lag. The Committee
would, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should initiate action, both statutory and
administrative, to facilitate timely maintenance and submission of accurate information and its
incorporation in both the Central Registers of the Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy.
The Committee would like to be apprised of the action initiated in this regard.

Issues concerning regulation of Naturopathy and Yoga
63. On being asked whether there is any mechanism in place for registration of Practitioners of Naturopathy
and Yoga, the Committee has been informed that presently there was no provision for registration of
Naturopathy & Yoga practitioners at Central Government level. However, some of the State Governments
like Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamilnadu, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and West Bengal
have provision for registration of such practitioners for BNYS graduates. The Central Government had
issued guidelines in the year 2006. In 2014 again, the Ministry had circulated a concept note on this subject
to all the State Governments, Universities & Colleges, and other stake holders. Based on the feedback
received in response thereto, the shape and structure of future mechanism for registration is under deliberation.
The then Department of AYUSH had decided in 2006, not to regulate Yoga and Naturopathy at Central level
on the basis of the following considerations:
(a) The CCIM did not agree to the proposed inclusion of Yoga and Naturopathy in their mandate
on the plea that it had nothing common with other systems namely Ayurveda, Siddha and
Unani.
(b) Setting up of separate Central Council for Yoga and Naturopathy was not agreed to on the
grounds that there were only few practitioners in the field of Yoga and Naturopathy and limited
infrastructure, which does not justify a separate Regulatory Body.
64. The Ministry also informed the Committee that the issue of regulation of Yoga & Naturopathy is
under deliberation.
65. The Committee observes that Naturopathy and Yoga are gaining popularity not only amongst
the Indians but all over the world and feels that there is an urgent need to regulate the practice of
Naturopathy and Yoga. Some guidelines/norms should be prescribed in this regard and the people
should be made aware of the benefit of these practices but under the guidance of the trained
manpower.

92. The increasing global interest in natural remedies has increased the demand for medicinal plants. The
resource base for AYUSH is largely plants which are largely sourced from the wild areas. This has led to the
emergence of a number of issues like sustainability, conservation, cultivation, quality assurance, protection

matters, Government of India established the National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB) under the Department

plants in the country and provides financial support to programmes relating to conservation, cultivation and
the all-round development of the medicinal plants sector.

Quality Control of ASU&H Drugs
101. As per information furnished to the Committee, the Ministry of AYUSH has a Drug Regulatory Cell.
The Cell is responsible for handling regulatory and quality control matters of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and
Homoeopathy (ASU and H) drugs. The AYUSH system of Medicine is governed by the Drugs and Cosmetics
Act 1940 and the Rules thereunder. Enforcement of the provisions contained under Chapter IV A of the Act
is the responsibility of the State Governments. In superintending the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics
Act, 1940 and Rules thereunder and Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954 in
relation to ASU and H drugs, the Drug Control Cell coordinates with the State Licensing Authorities and
Drug Controllers to achieve uniform administration of the legal provisions and for providing regulatory
guidance and clarification to the States. It also undertakes program management and examination of State
Annual Plans for Quality Control under National AYUSH Mission (NAM) through which grant-in-aid is
provided for improving infrastructure and functional capacity of Drug Testing Laboratories, Pharmacies
and Enforcement Mechanism in the States.
102. During the course of examination of Demands for Grants (2013-14) the Ministry of AYUSH (erstwhile
Department of AYUSH) had admitted that due to weak organizational set-ups in the State AYUSH Directorates
and Licensing Authorities, the utilization of grants released under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for
Quality Control has not been up to the mark. The problem of non-submission of Utilization Certificates
deprived the States of availing any more financial assistance for improving the quality control measures. The
compliance to Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) by ASU and H drug manufacturers and its enforcement
by the State regulators is not in the desired perspective. Besides, drug testing facilities in the States are
inadequate to meet the regulatory needs because of the infrastructural bottlenecks in the State Drugs Testing
Laboratories and scarcity of Approved Drug Testing Laboratories and Capacities.
103. On being asked about the allocation for quality control of AYUSH drugs for 2015-16, the Secretary
during his evidence replied that out of Rs. 318.00 Crore allocated for the Centrally Sponsored Schemes
about sixteen crores of rupees will be available for the quality control of AYUSH drugs for all the States
together, which will work out to Rs. 20.00 to Rs. 30.00 Lakhs for each State.
104. In reply to a question the Ministry has informed that 19 proposals from 19 States have been received
out of which proposals from 12 States, viz. Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh,
Rajasthan, Tripura, West Bengal, Haryana and Arunachal Pradesh, Assam and Andaman Nicobar Islands
have been approved and the proposal of remaining 7 States, viz. Punjab, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Jharkhand,
Karnataka, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir are yet to be approved by NAM.
105. The Committee in its 55th Report on Demands for Grants (2012-13) of erstwhile Department
of AYUSH had inter alia observed that "the quality and standardization of ASU&H products and
stringent implementation of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and the rules
framed thereunder are very vital for the credibility o ASU and H drugs. However, the drug testing
requirements of ASU and H drugs cannot be me without setting up adequate number of quality
control laboratories and strengthenin of the enforcement mechanisms of the States." From
information made available b the Committee, it is revealed that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme
for supportin quality control activities has been evaluated by an external agency and revised suitabi
on the basis of suggestions from the States. The Committee sincerely hopes that th revised scheme
would maximize outcome oriented implementation and lead to bette off-take under this scheme
during the remaining period of the 12th Five Year Plan. Th Committee recommends that the Ministry
should closely monitor utilization of th funds under this head particularly, as it relates to capacity
building of the State Dru Testing Laboratories for better quality control of ASU and H drugs.

26
The Committee also notes that Indian Ayurvedic drugs were found containing excessive mercury
and other substance and therefore were banned by Eurpoean Union and some other Countries and

106. On being asked about the updated status of setting up a Central Regulatory Authority for ASU and H
Drugs and creating the Central Drug Controller for Ayurveda; Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs, the
Ministry in a written reply has stated th following:-
"Note for seeking approval of the Cabinet to set up a separate Central Drugs Controller of
AYUSH was sent to the Cabinet Secretariat on 9th October, 2014. The note has been received
back on 11.2.2015 with the advice from PMO for Minister of Health and Family Welfare to
hold a meeting with Secretary (AYUSH), Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and
Drug Controller General of India to consider and recommend whether a full-fledged Drug
Controller General for AYUSH is required or whether there is possibility of a wing for AYUSH,
manned by experts from AYUSH field placed under the existing Drug Controller General of
India. Meeting was held on 05.03.2015 wherein it was decided to develop a vertical structure
of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) headed by
Drugs Controller General (India)".
107. During the course of examination of Demands for Grants (2013-14), the Ministry of AYUSH, on
being asked as to why it is not desirable to let CDSCO regulate ASU Drugs, had submitted that CDSCO has
been basically dealing with quality control of allopathic drugs and accordingly, the whole paraphernalia there
does not have the wherewithal to effectively regulate ASU&H drugs. The basic reason is that ASU&H drugs
are distinct from allopathic drugs in terms of philosophy, principles, concepts, standards, quality aspects,
applications, numbers and count of manufacturing units and testing requirements, hence they need to have
different regulations. Inspite of common Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the regulatory issues of ASU&H
drugs are not being taken care of by the Central Drugs Controller Office due to non-availability of requisite
expertise and huge workload of matters related to allopathic drugs. The idea of having a common Central
Drugs Authority with Additional Drug Controller of AYUSH had not been earlier agreed to. However, the
office of the Drug Controller General (India) was strengthened by sanctioning 175 posts for modern medicine
and was renamed as Central Drugs Standards Control Organisation (CDSCO), but no posts were sanctioned
for the Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy. It was thereafter only that in accordance with the
recommendations of a high powered Committee and ASU Drugs Consultative Committee and considering
the specific regulatory requirements of ASU&H drugs, setting up a separate Central Drugs Controller of
AYUSH was found to be a necessary requirement.
108. The Committee observes that quality control and standardization of ASU&H drugs leaves
much to be desired. It has often been reported in the media that Ayurveda and Homoeopathy drugs,
which were given to patients for various ailments, were laced with steroids and other improper
drugs. Permissible limits of heavy metals, pesticide residue, microbial load etc. are also sometimes
breached and regulatory needs of standardization and quality control of ASU&H drugs get seriously
impaired. On the issue of setting up of a separate Drug Controller of AYUSH, the decision to
develop a vertical structure of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(CDSCO) headed by the Drug Controller General of India is not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee feels that in order to strengthen regulatory mechanism and effectively oversee the
quality control of ASU&H drugs, setting up of a separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs

27
is an imminent necessity since a wing of AYUSH in the existing CDSCO may not produce the
desired result of effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. The Committee is of the view that a separate
Central Drugs Controller of AYUSH will help synergise the core competencies of the Central and
State Regulatory Authorities by developing dynamic relation between them and also go a long way
in building credibility in ASU&H drugs besides promoting AYUSH in foreign countries. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that action be initiated to set up an independent and separate Central Drug
Controller for ASU&H drugs at the earliest.

iv. In addition, the Ministry of AYUSH has signed MoUs for setting up Unani and Ayurveda Chair
at the Premier Institutes in South Africa; Ayurveda Chair at Trinidad and Tobago and Hungary".
122. The Committee observes that though some headway has been made towards signing of MOUs
for co-operation in the traditional systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy with developed countries
having credible regulatory framework, a lot still remains to be done for tangible progress in this
matter. Needless to emphasise that the Ministry should continue to focus its energies on the developed
European countries and the USA for entering into MOUs so that the therapeutic credentials of
AYUSH systems of Medicine can be established globally.

strengths of AYUSH systems by using outdoor, electronic media including organization of Arogya fairs and
