NEW ISSUES
V. Referral System
4.26 The Committee was given to understand by reply of IMA that the referral system for
CGHS beneficiaries is complex and unclear. This was pursued with the Department in
response to which it was clarified that the beneficiaries have to be referred by the
Dispensary to a Government specialist only. The Government specialist decides upon the line
of treatment to be followed and the beneficiary thereafter has the option of undergoing this
procedure/treatment in any empanelled hospital of his choice / Government hospital. It was
also submitted that Private hospitals are empanelled under CGHS for inpatient treatment only.
Limited facilities are provided for OPD consultation in empanelled hospitals. Post-operative
OPD follow up treatment is permitted for six conditions, where the initial treatment was
taken with prior permission and permission was obtained for post-operative. These are
cancer treatment, cardiac surgery, Kidney transplantation, Hip/Knee joint replacement and
post trauma cases. In addition, beneficiaries of satellite towns of DeIhi- Noida, Faridabad,
Ghaziabad and Gurgaon are also permitted OPD consultation since there is dearth of
Government hospitals/specialists in these towns. In all such cases, where OPD consultation
is permitted the advice of the specialist of empanelled hospital is treated like that of a
Government specialist.
4.27 It was also informed that orders have also been issued whereby beneficiaries who
have taken inpatient medical treatment from a CGHS empanelled hospital will be issued
medicines from the treating private hospital at the time of discharge, for a period upto seven
(7) days.
Further Recommendation
4.28 The Committee is of the view that the referral system in CGHS is a time
consuming process and the Department, therefore, needs to simplify the procedure so
that precious time is not lost in getting all the permissions and approvals repeatedly.
The Committee suggests that the beneficiary should be given the option to choose from
getting treatment done from Government Hospital Empanelled Hospitals after consulting
the doctor at CGHS wellness centres.

43
VI. Cashless Facilities to CGHS Pensioners
4.29 The Committee came to know from a recent Media report that the Ministry has now
decided to stop CGHS cashless scheme presently available to the pensioners and their
dependents from March 7, 2014. Due to this the pensioners and their dependants are going to
suffer the most, keeping in view the higher cost of different packages, as most of the
pensioners cannot afford such a huge amount for their treatment. The Committee taking a
serious view of the above developments observes that the Ministry cannot escape from its
social responsibility of providing free health care facilities to the CGHS beneficiaries,
particularly the pensioners and their dependents. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends the Ministry to withdraw the decision of stopping cashless facilities to the
pensioners immediately.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS - AT A GLANCE
The Committee is constrained to note that out of sanctioned strength of 1620
General Duty Medical Officers and Specialists, as many as 282 posts are lying vacant
and 240 have been filled on contract basis. The Committee understands that the
Department of Health and Family Welfare has attempted to bridge the gap by appointing
doctors and specialists on contract as a stop gap arrangement. But the Committee is of
the opinion that this could not be a long term solution to the problem of chronic
shortage of doctors and the Department needs to address it with urgency since without
the availability of doctors, all existing infrastructure of CGHS will not guarantee
healthcare to the beneficiaries. From the information shared with the Committee, it is
evident that even if UPSC makes selection of doctors, very few join CGHS. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department undertake a thorough study to
find out the reasons behind this trend and take remedial action accordingly. The
Committee would like to be apprised of the initiatives taken by the Department to
attract doctors and paramedical staff to join CGHS.  (Para 3.7)
Complaints like frequent failure of electricity, non-operational generator, age old
furniture, irregular supply of sanitation materials have been brought to the notice of
the Committee in some of the Wellness Centres running through rented accomodation.
The Committee is dismayed to know the sorry state of affairs in such centres. The
Committee is of the opinion that urgent interim measures are required for proper
maintenance of basic infrastructure in dispensaries functioning in rented
accommodations till buildings specially designed for dispensary are constructed. Basic
amenities should be ensured in the dispensaries working through rented accommodation.

proposed to be taken on rent for opening CGHS Wellness Centre should be made to see
whether it meets the desired parameters so as to avoid any inconvenience at later stage.

to ensure regular water and electricity supply. (Para 3.17)

upon the issue of providing regular homoeopathy services at all Wellness Centres, as
recommended in para 50 of the 71
st  Report. The Committee would have desired an
action plan from the Ministry in this regard and is perturbed to note the evasive
reply in the matter. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation
on the need of providing regular Homoeopathy services at all the Wellness Centres.
The Committee would appreciate a time bond action in the matter from the
Department.  (para 3.21)

medicines / treatment procedures; putting in place transparency measures like putting up status
of medical reimbursement claims, claims of pensioners pending for more than 30 days; details
of payments in preceding month to empanelled hospitals/laboratories on CGHS website.

PART A (HEALTH SECTOR) 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATION IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
I   BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.16) 
1.1 The Committee notes that due to broad budget ary cuts imposed by the Ministry of 
Finance, fifteen important Health Schemes of the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare 
have been left without any budgetary provisions for 2015 -16. The Committee also notes 
that Ministry has furnished a list of nine scheme s of tertiary care (Table No. 2), which in 
the opinion of the Ministry are essential for correcting the existing imbalances in tertiary 
healthcare and therefore non-negotiable from the point of view of budgetary support but for 
which no funds have been allotted for 2015-16. The Committee is appreciative of the fiscal 
constraints faced by the Ministry of Finance due to moderation in economic growth and the 
impact of global slowdown. But given the fact that public funding is estimated to be of the 
order of on ly 19.67% of the expenses of healthcare in the country [as per National Health 
Accounts Estimates (2004 -05)] and most of private expenditure is Out -of-Pocket (OOP) 
expense which has the potential of pushing even the non -poor into poverty, the Committee 
is of the firm view that starving the above said health schemes of budgetary support may 
have catastrophic implications for the expansion of tertiary care facilities and equitable 
distribution of tertiary care to different segments of population. Keeping in v iew the 
slightly tight fiscal space the Government is in and seeking to strike a balance between 
public good and the need for containing fiscal deficit, the Committee recommends that out 
of the nine schemes indicated by the Ministry for providing budgetary outlay, the following 
five schemes are of critical importance: (i) Trauma Care (Capacity Building for 
Developing Trauma Care facilities in Govt. Hospitals on National Highways); (ii) National 
Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardi ovascular Diseases and 
Stroke; (iii) Health Care for Elderly; (iv) National Programme for Control of Blindness; 
and (v) Human Resource for Health. This recommendation of the Committee warrants 
utmost attention of Ministry of Finance. The Committee would li ke the Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare to bring this recommendation to the notice of the Ministry of Finance 
with a sense of urgency and expediency and apprise the Committee of the follow -up action 
taken by them (i.e. Ministry of Finance). If adequat e budgetary provisions are not made for 

these schemes, the Committee may call the Secretary to acquaint itself with the reasons 
behind non allocation of funds for the schemes. 
Action Taken 
1.2 The Ministry of Finance has been apprised of the recommendation  of the 
Committee. 
 
1.3 Moreover, with a view to emphasise the need for allocation for the schemes of 
critical importance a D.O. reference was made  to the Ministry of Finance by Secretary 
(H&FW), wherein it was categorically mentioned that the primary and  secondary sector 
only could be part of  NHM.  The Tertiary sector being part of Health could not be 
subsumed with NHM and  it required additional funds to support ongoing activities which 
were  being continued from the eleventh plan and  there are committ ed liabilities.  
Accordingly, Supplementary Demand has been projected to the Ministry of Finance for 
consideration by Parliament during ensuing Monsoon Session.  The proposal seeks funds 
for the Schemes of critical importance, viz. (i) Assistance for Capac ity Building for 
Developing Trauma Care facilities in Govt. Hospitals on National Highways; (ii) National 
Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardio Vascular Disease and 
Stroke; (iii) Health Care for Elderly; (iv) National Programme f or Control of Blindness; 
and (v) Human Resources for Health & Medical Education. 
 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.18) 
1.4 The Committee also takes note of the Health Secretary‟s submission that there is a 
changeover from society route of funds to treasury route of funds. The Committee observes 
that with this changeover, UCs conditionality will no longer be an absolute bar for release 
of funds. The Committee hopes that this will have positive bearing on better utilization of 
budgeted funds as well a timely release of the funds. Though the changeover from society 
mode to treasury mode has been made for the purpose of better utilization of funds, the 
Committee would like the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to be vigilant and ensure 
that this chang eover does not lead to fiscal profligacy and funds so released result in 
corresponding benefits and assets creation on the ground. The Committee takes note of the 
Health Secretary's submission that this changeover has resulted in delay in transfer of funds  

to the Health Societies. The Committee would like the Ministry to initiate immediate 
remedial measures in coordination with the States and quickly iron out the hindrances 
coming in the way of speedy transfer of Central funds to the State Health Societies. 
Action Taken 
1.5 The Observation of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  In this regard  
the matter has since been taken up at higher levels with the State and U.T. Governments 
requesting them to ensure release from consolidated fund of States to State Health Societies 
(SHS) within 15 days of receipt of funds from Govt. of India, failing which they are liable 
for payment of penal interest.  The release of 2 nd tranche of funds is also contingent on the 
transfer of 1 st tranche of funds to SHS.  Tim ely availability of funds with State Health 
Societies is critical to effective implementation of  Programmes/Schemes in the States. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.27) 
1.6 A perusal of Annexure 1 reveals that in the Plan provision of the Health Secto r for 
2013-14, the actual expenditure was Rs. 4205.74 crore as against the BE of Rs. 8166.00 
crore which was reduced to  Rs. 5065.00 crore at RE stage. In 2014 -15 also, the actual 
expenditure has been Rs. 3457.49 crore as against the BE of Rs. 8733.00 cror e which was 
reduced to Rs. 6772.18 crore at the RE stage. The Committee is dismayed to observe that 
the slippages in utilization of the budgeted funds must have had an adverse bearing on 
moving towards the avowed objective of universal health coverage for the populace of the 
country. The Committee in its 67 th Report on Demands for Grants 2013 -14 had expressed 
concern at occurrence of huge savings and recommended that the Department should take 
concrete steps to ensure proper utilization of funds by means of  prudent assessment of the 
fund requirements and design effective mechanism to make a balance between spending 
and savings. The Committee again expresses its displeasure at substantial and recurrent 
underutilization of the allocated funds and observes that  such a state of affairs is indicative 
of serious shortcomings in budgetary planning and monitoring of utilization of the 
budgeted funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends that realistic projection of fund 
requirements should be given utmost priority at  the highest level of the Ministry and 
periodic meetings should be held to review and constantly monitor the progress of 
expenditure so that large variations in the BE,RE and AE could be avoided. 
Action Taken 
1.7 The recommendations of the Committee has be en noted for compliance.  The actual 
expenditure during 2014 -15 was Rs. 5645.37 crores against RE of Rs. 6772.18 crore. The 

shortfall in expenditure is mainly attributed to non -receipt of UCs from the grantee bodies 
resulting in release of lesser grants.  The expenditure position is regularly monitored in the 
Senior Officers‟ meeting taken by Secretary on weekly basis. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.30) 
1.8 The Committee takes note of the submission that a number of schemes/programmes 
were merged in certain pools for optimum utilization of budgetary assumptions‟ and feels 
that there is a need to carry out an appraisal of the efficacy of the new measures initiated 
and formulate remedial measures based on the findings for better financial performance. 
The Committee would like to be kept apprised of the efficacy of the new measures initiated 
for better utilization of budgetary provisions.  
 
Action Taken 
1.9 The Observation of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  However,   as 
schemes have been merged in certain pools for the first time, the efficacy of new measures 
so  initiated, would be reviewed/assessed after the close of the current financial year 2015 -
16. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.33) 
1.10 The Committee takes note of the submission of the Ministry that the main reason for 
under-utilization of funds under Health Sector has been non -settlement of Utilization 
Certificates (UCs). Though some measures have been taken to liquidate pending UCs, 
given the fact that a substantial amount to  the tune of Rs 2,196.95 crore is still involved in 
pending UCs and the pending UCs date as far back as year 1993, it is obvious that a lot still 
remains to be done. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should put in 
place a dedicated mec hanism in this regard to ensure that all pending UCs are liquidated 
within a period of six months. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the action 
taken and the outcomes thereof within a period of three months from the date of 
presentation of this Report. 
 
Action Taken 
1.11 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  However, 
in this regard it may be pertinent to mention here that State Governments are reminded 
during various review meetings to furnish pending UCs for settl ement within the fixed time 
frame. Letters and reminders to State Government are sent regularly to furnish pending 

UCs.  Special drives are being launched to reconcile and settle UCs with State 
Governments. 
 
II SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL & VARDHMAN MAHAVIR MEDICA L     
COLLEGE (SJH & VMMC), NEW DELHI 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 2.3) 
1.12 The Committee observes that in the year 2014-15, the BE of Rs. 330.00 crore for the 
Safdarjung Hospital was increased to Rs. 580.90 crore at RE stage but the actual 
expenditure is Rs. 310.22 crore as on  5th March, 2015 and is likely to be around the BE, 
given the trend of expenditure witnessed so far. The Committee would, therefore, like to be 
apprised of all the factors warranting increase in budgetary provisions at RE sta ge and the 
reasons for not utilizing the enhanced allocations. 
Action Taken 
1.13 The total budget provision of Rs. 330 crore was enhanced to Rs. 580.90 crore at RE 
stage in view of the requirement of redevelopment plan, likely joining of new employees, 
etc. This was revised at FE stage to Rs. 562.71 crore, out of which Rs. 562.12 crore was 
utilised by the Hospital by 31.3.2015. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 2.5) 
1.14 The Committee would like to be informed of (i) the total expenditure incurred on 
the Re-development of the Hospital vis-à-vis the total approved outlay for the project in the 
Twelfth Plan; (ii) the total surrenders of the budgeted plan funds under this head; (iii) 
whether all the required approvals for the Project had been obtained; (iv) t he original cost 
of the Project and the revised cost, if any, and (v) the original time -line for completion of 
the project. 
Action Taken 
1.15 The information is given below: 
(i)       Government has approved a redevelopment plan of Safdarjung Hospital with a 
total estimated cost of Rs. 1333 crore. Out of Rs. 1333 crore, Rs. 349.94 crore 
has been released so far.  
(ii)       No fund meant for the redevelopment has been surrendered.  
(iii)  The construction work of Redevelopment Plan is already going on after 
obtaining approval of the competent authority. 
(iv) The original estimates approved for redevelopment work phase I of Safdarjung 
Hospital is Rs. 1333 crore. Presently, there is no case of revised cost.  

 
1.16 The original time-line for completion of the project is March, 2017. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 2.6) 
1.17 The Committee is unable to comprehend as to why there was non -availability of 
funds when the RE of Rs. 580.90 crore was steeply higher than the actuals of Rs. 310.22 
crore. The Committee would like the Ministry to clarify the position in unambiguous terms.

1.18 The total budget provision of Rs. 330 crore was enhanced to Rs. 580.90 crore at RE 
stage in view of the requirement of redevelopment plan, joining of new employees, etc. 
The budget provision for major works was Rs. 100 crore for the year 2014 -15. M/s HSCC,

crore for redevelopment plan.  Approval for Rs.215.00 Cr. for redevelopment plan was

Recommendation/Observation (para no 2.13) 
1.19 The Committee takes note of the measures taken/being taken by the Department to 
fill up the vacant posts. Taking into account the fact that there is huge mismatch between 
requirement and availability of doctors, the Committee recommend s that it would require 
more measures than merely modifying Recruitment Rules to attract more doctors to 
Safdarjung Hospital. The Committee, therefore, directs the Department to pay adequate 
attention for making the pay packages being offered and service c onditions to doctors more 
attractive.   
Action Taken

Central Government. Following the recommendation of the 5th CPC, the promotion of 
doctors was made time -bound upto  NFSG level without linkage to vacancies under the

the talent.  
 

1.21 The Government has now set -up 7th CPC for revising salaries of Central 
Government employees. The concerned Division has already submitted its comments on 
the demand of doctors service association related to enhancement/ revision of pay 
packages. Further action in the matter may be taken only after receipt of recommendations 
of 7th CPC.

I   BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.15) 
3.1 The Committee views with serious concern the sharp reductions in allocations of 
funds for Health and NHM in the Central Plan in 2015 -16 and feels that huge assumption 
has been made that 42 per cent transfer of Central Taxes to the States in the form of untied 
funds would compensate for the shortfall in Central funds for Health and if this assumption 
is not validated, then there will be a very severe shortfall of health expenditure in several 
backward States which fare poorly in terms of various health indicators and are, therefore, 
required to increase their health expenditure, but are unable to do so due to various reasons. 
The past experience shows that if the spending is left to the States, contractor -intensive 
sectors takes priority over non -contractor intensive sectors and Health, not being a 
contractor intensive sector, will take a backseat in such circumstances. The increase in 
education expenditure that took place from the mid 80s, in many ways, forced the States to 
make an increase in their expenditure commensurately and one of the objectives of the 
National Rural Health Mission which has now become the National Health Mission is to 
spur the States to spend more on health. The Committee also takes note of the fact that a a 
number of States have already presented their Budgets for the financial year 2015 -16 and 
no budgetary provisions have been made therein for meeting the shortfall in expenditure on 
key health  schemes. Also, given the precarious state of  States' finances, expecting the 
States to allocate adequate financial resources for health for the financial year 2015 -16 is 
unrealistic. Keeping all these factors in view, the Committee apprehends that in the 
financial year 2015 -16, targeted health outco mes would be seriously jeopardized if the 
Central Government does not move quickly towards shouldering a bigger share in overall 
public spending on health. The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of 
depending on the States for additional resources for health, in the year 2015-16, the Central 
Government should enumerate a fiscal roadmap for generating and allocating more 
financial resources for health so that the vision of moving towards universalization of 
affordable healthcare is translated into reality. The Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry institute a regular system of review with states so that an up -to-date assessment is 

always available on whether states are indeed allocating resources to health as the Central 
government is hoping. The Committee would like to be kept informed about such 
assessments on a regular basis. 
Action Taken 
3.2 The Central Governments budgetary allocation for the health sector for the year 
2015-16 is Rs. 24549.00 crore as against Rs.24400.00 crore in 2014 -15 ( RE). The 
relevance of efficiency in public spending   for optimum utilisation of available resources 
for maximum outcome is brought to focus, in the endeavour of the Central Government to 
supplement the resources of the state for health spending. 
 
3.3 Presently the share of Centre to State in the total public spending on health is 
approximately in the ratio of 31:69. In this backdrop, the recommendation of the 
Fourteenth Finance Commission would allow states greater autonomy in financing and 
designing of schemes as per their needs. The change in devolution pattern to states in 2015 -
16 is expected to result in a year on year increase of Rs 1.78 lakh crores approximately. 
This fiscal space can be used by states for increased spending in the health sector.  The  
Ministry of Finance has been addressed to provide additional funds through Supplementary 
Demands for Grants (2015-16). 
 
3.4 The NHM framework provides guidance to states in planning financing and 
executing, programmes/ schemes for district and below healt h care interventions. 
Financing and support to states under NHM to strengthen public health systems and health 
care delivery is based on the State‟s Programme Implementation Plan(PIP) which provides 
states the flexibility  to plan and implement state speci fic action plans within the broad 
national parameters and priorities. The MOUs signed with States, the outcomes expected 
from financial investments and the institutional reforms to strengthen State health systems 
would be the guiding factor towards achievement of targeted outcomes.   
 
3.5 The NHM framework provides for monitoring and evaluation as a continuous 
process. Regular monitoring visits from National Programme Management Units to States 
and districts/cities, community monitoring of facilities suppor ted by NGOs, along with a 
system of periodic concurrent audit and an annual audit are envisaged to strengthen 
accountability.  

 
Further Recommendation 
3.6 While making the recommendation in para 1.15 of Part A of its 82 nd Report , 
the Committee had emphasi zed that the Centre should not abdicate its responsibility 
of paying for a critical sector like Health entirely to the States as Health being a non -
contractor sector, remains at the fringe of budgetary priorities and therefore, fails to 
get adequate alloca tions. The Committee had also stressed the fact that none of the 
States had budgeted for the increase in allocation for health for the financial year 
2015-16 despite a 10% increase in the States share post new tax devolution formula,  
putting the targeted health outcomes in serious jeopardy.  The Committee is 
constrained to observe that instead of vigorously pursuing with Ministry of Finance to 
address the concerns of the Committee with regard to inadequate health financing for 
the Financial Year 2015 -16 and formulating its reply accordingly, the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare has chosen to harp on the "relevance of efficiency in 
public spending" and "the change in devolution pattern to states (by way of increase 
in transfer of taxes to States from 32% to 42%) and the resultant flexibility to the 
States to decide on increased spending in the health sector". The Committee observes 
that despite the  new  Centre -State tax sharing model, several of the States are 
complaining that they are worse off in th e new dispensation as they see a reduction in 
their share of central funds -under the new devolution formula. The Committee 
observes that health is pivotal to development. As per the draft National Health Policy 
put out in January 2015, over 63 million peop le in India face the threat of poverty 
each year due to unaffordable health care expenditure. The Committee therefore 
apprehends that the drastic slashing of Central budgetary support to States for health 
sector will further accentuate the problem and have  catastrophic consequences. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends with all the power at its command that the 
Department should once again impress upon the Ministry of Finance the imperative 
of providing additional financial resources for health for the fina ncial year 2015 -16 
through Supplementary Demand for Grants. The Committee would like the 
Department to report to it the progress made in the matter within a period of one 
month from the presentation of this Report. 
3.7 Furthermore, the Committee notes with dismay that on its recommendation for 
instituting a regular review system with states for assessing whether they are indeed 

allocating additional resources for health, post the 10% increase in devolution of 
central tax share to States, the Department has replied in a generic manner. The 
Committee while deprecating the Department for showing such casual approach 
recommends that an assessment be made urgently and communicated to the 
Committee as to what extent the 10% rise in States revenue is reflected in t he 
allocation of additional resources for health by them. 
3.8 The Committee also recommends that in order to optimally utilize the available 
financial resources, the Department of Health and Family Welfare in co -ordination 
with States should develop a para digm of technical process so as to track and report 
the flow of funds from Centre and States to health sector. 
 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.19) 
3.9 The Committee observes from the information furnished that as per the Twelfth 
Five Year Plan docum ent, the total public funding by the Centre and the States, both Plan 
and Non-Plan, on core health issues is envisaged to increase to 1.87 per cent of the GDP by 
the end of the Twelfth Plan, but for the BE 2014 -15, this figure is 1.2 per cent of the GDP. 
The budget allocation for the fourth year of the Twelfth Plan, i.e. 2015 -16, is also almost 
1.2 per cent of GDP. Three years of the 12th Five Year Plan has already elapsed and only 
two years are left. This implies that the target of government spending of 1 .87 per cent of 
GDP on core health will not be achieved. The Committee observes that the existing per 
capita public spending on health is low which raises serious doubts on achieving the goals 
of raising the total Government expenditure on the broader Heal th Sector to 2.5% of GDP 
by the end of the 12th Plan. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government 
should chalk out a solid fiscal roadmap for generating and allocating additional financial 
resources for health so that the States are provided a muc h larger resource envelope for 
health and the urgency of raising government spending on health to 2 -3 % of GDP is also 
not lost sight of. 
Action Taken 
3.10 The Department of Health and Family Welfare has sought for additional financial 
resources as supplem entary grants from the Ministry of Finance. Health being a State 
subject, the Central Government supplements the efforts of the State Governments through 
financial and technical assistance. The Central allocation of funds for health sector is based 
inter-alia on the availability of resources and competing claims on these resources.. 

Further Recommendation 
3.11 The Committee, observes that for the delivery of high quality health care, 
public health spending on primary, secondary and tertiary health care will  need to 
rise substantially as compared to what it is today. With public spending on health 
being just 1.2% of GDP in India, our country lags behind China (2.9%) and Brazil 
(4.1%). With the current economic growth of the country pegged in the range of 7 to  
7.5 %, it is abundantly clear that our public spending on health is not commensurate 
with our economic progress.  As per media reports, India lags behind countries like 
Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and even Nepal in health indicators like infant mortality rate, 
child immunization rate and  total life expectancy. The Committee is of the 
considered view that if unmet health care needs are to be addressed,  Health sector 
cannot be placed at the fringe of budgetary planning in the name of " availability of 
resources and competing claims on these resources". The Committee, therefore, lends 
its full parliamentary support to the Department of Health and Family Welfare in its 
request for additional financial resources through supplementary grants. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.24) 
3.12 The Committee is dismayed to note that huge savings have been registered in the 
Capital Account during the last two years. Such gross under -utilization of funds under 
Capital Section of the Demands for Grants points to the fact that development oriented 
activities have been seriously impaired. The Committee, therefore, observes that the 
occurrence of huge savings on the Capital Account warrants special attention and proactive 
steps by the Ministry so that this pernicious trend could be tackled in an effective manner. 
Action Taken 
3.13 The savings under Capital Section is mainly due to slow progress in Capital works  
and procurement of equipments under the schemes viz. Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha 
Yojana, (including New AIIMS) (Rs. 979.02 Cr., and Institutions of Higher Learning as 
per Oversight Committee. (Rs. 83.13 Cr.).   
 
Further Recommendation 
3.14 While making the recommendation in para 1.24 of Part A of its 82 nd report, the 
Committee had expected the Department of Health and F amily Welfare to take 
appropriate measures to ensure that the budgeted funds do not remain locked up by 
way of huge savings, that too on the Capital Account. The Committee, therefore, 

regrets to note that the Department has merely chosen to attribute the o ccurrence of 
savings on the Capital Account to the slow progress in Capital works and delay in 
procurement of equipments under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana. 
The Committee is of the view that had the Department shown even a modicum of 
seriousness in coordinating with the concerned officials dealing with capital works 
and procurement of equipments and taken timely measures to overcome the 
shortcomings noticed, the budgeted funds would not have been surrendered  later on. 
The Committee, therefor e, once again urges the Department to take effective steps to 
squarely  address the recurring problem of delays and cost/time overruns in 
implementation of projects including PMSSY. 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 1.26)

Committee is constrained to observe that the Department has been lackadaisical in its 
approach in t he matter and not done due diligence, resulting in delay in conceptualization 
and finalization of this Project. Now that the Government has accorded its "in -principle" 
approval to the Re -development Plan of Dr. RML Hospital, the Committee would expect 
the Department to quickly complete all approval -related formalities and take concrete steps 
towards translating the vision of Redevelopment into reality. The Committee desires to be 
kept apprised of the developments in this regard. 
Action Taken 
3.29 The original plan drawn earlier envisaged construction of Super Speciality Block at 
an area of land measuring 3.99 acres at G -point. However, on re -survey of the land, which

at G-point, 1.74 acres of land belongs to the President‟s Estate. Therefore, revised plan for

Further Recommendation 
3.31 The Committee is happy to note that some forward movement has been 
reported in the construction of Super Specialty Block at Dr. RML Hospital. However, 
there is still a long way to go before this project will reach its logical culmination. The 
Committee would like the Department to put in place a focused monitoring 
mechanism to ensure that this long -pending project is speeded up. The Committee 
also recommends that the Depar tment proactively pursue obtaining of all necessary 
clearances to avoid further delay in implementation of the Project.

Further Recommendation 
3.39    The Committee is constrained to observe that this is a typical case of 
procrastination. Despite the fact that the construction work regardin g the 
Redevelopment Plan of LMHC and Associated Hospitals has been "at a standstill" 
for more than a year and the contractor M/s Unity Infra Projects has failed to honour 
the commitments made by it on multiple occasions earlier, the Department has not 
been able to take any decisive penal action against the Contractor and "issuance of 
termination letter is under consideration." The Committee is seriously concerned that 
so much time has already elapsed but the Redevelopment Project is unlikely to be 
executed within the designated timeline and the delay is also likely to entail cost 
overrun. While taking a serious view in the matter, the Committee recommends that 
stringent measures be taken against the Contractor M/s Unity Infra Projects, which 
could inter alia  include,  stiff penalty for violation of terms of the contract and 
blacklisting of the contractor. The Committee also recommends that prompt action be 
taken to award the contract to a reputed contractor who is capable of handling the 
construction work and  speeding up execution of the Redevelopment Plan within the 
approved cost.  
V        ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS), NEW DELHI 
 
Recommendation/Observation (para no 5.3) 
3.40 The Committee notes the assertion of the Department that the enti re grant of Rs. 
343.00 crore was likely to be spent by the end of the financial year 2014 -15, as against the 
allocation of Rs. 343.00 crore in RE 2014 -15 for creation of capital assets, the expenditure 
incurred till February was only Rs. 108.70 crore (31.6 %) and Rs. 243.30 crore (i.e. 68.4%) 
was left unspent. Given the fact that as per the norms stipulated by the Ministry of Finance, 
not more than 15% can be spent in the last month of the financial year, the Committee 
wonders as to how the Department would be able to achieve the feat of spending Rs. 
243.30 crore (68.4%) in the last month without violating the provisions of General 

Financial Rules. The Committee would like the Department to explain the dichotomy in 
this regard. 
Action Taken 
3.41 Total expenditure of Rs 191.69 crore was incurred under Plan during the month of 
March on procurement of machinery and equipments and execution of capital projects.  
The broad reasons for substantial expenditures in the month of March, 2015 are as under: 
 
(i) The requirement of Machinery & Equipments of each Centre/Department in AIIMS 
is assessed by a multimember Assessment Committee in the beginning of the financial year 
and funds allocation is made accordingly.   
 
(ii) This is followed by finalisation of technical spe cifications. As in most of the cases 
technical specifications of the highly sophisticated and specialized in nature. These are 
finalized by the month of August. For the equipments costing above Rs 30 lakh, external 
experts are also associated in preparation of technical specifications. 
 
(iii) All expenditure proposals including procurement and construction proposals costing 
Rs.5.00 Crore and above require approval of the Standing Finance Committee (SFC) 
Chaired by the Secretary, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare before finalizing the 
process. Convening meeting of SFC  also takes time. 
 
(iv) The institute floats tenders for different equipments.  Wide publicity of tenders is 
given and tender submission and analysis of bids takes time. Technical evaluation 
including demonstration of the equipments, wherever required, also takes time.  Then, the 
Store Purchase Committee meetings, Price Bid Opening meetings, Negotiations Meetings 
are held and also concurrence of Finance Division and approval of Competent Author ity is 
obtained before award of contracts, which is again a time consuming process but is 
essentially required in light of the provisions of GFR and CVC guidelines to ensure 
fairness and transparency in the procurement process.   
 
(v) In some cases,  re -tender has to be done due to single bid or inadequate competition 
with a view to generate more competition for which specifications are also sometimes  re -

visited and made  more broad based. Thus, majority of contracts reach their final stages 
only by the last quarter of the Financial Year. 
 
(vi) In case of indigenous equipments or imported equipments offered in Indian Rupees, 
generally a lead time of 1 -2 months is given to suppliers to supply the stores and 
accordingly the supplies are received in the months  of February-March. After the receipt of 
supplies and issuance of Inspection Notes, the payments are released.  
 
(vii) In case of imported equipments in foreign currency, the letters of credit are 
established through the State Bank of India, Foreign Exchan ge Division and they also 
require some processing time. Majority of the letters of credit are opened in the month of 
March only, which inflates the expenditure figures in the last month of the financial year.  
 
(viii) Expenditure on capital works is genera lly made on circumstantial need in line with 
the project/ work status. Payments are made against works already completed and for 
works which are taken up at the end of financial year.   
Further Recommendation 
3.42 The Committee takes note of the elaborate procedures laid down for the 
procurement of machinery and equipments, The Committee feels that given the 
protracted and procrastinated process of procurement of equipments, there is a need 
to carry out an appraisal of the extant procedures and take remedia l measures for 
simplification of the procedures so that the procurement process is not hamstrung. 
Steps should also be taken to minimize the possibility of fiscal slippage which is 
distinct in the current fiscal, and achieve the desired outcomes without co mpromising 
the quality of expenditures.

performance target, specific time target and specific cost target. But converting almost entire 
healthcare delivery system into a Mission by adding more and more schemes into the National 
Health Mission is making it unwieldy as well as p utting a question mark on its operational

National Health Mission and to make the Mission precise, more focused and manageable. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the structure of National Health Mission may be 
reviewed in order to make it more focused and precise. The Committee also recommends that a 
matrix may be provided on the uses of funds released and success made in achieving the health

2.6 The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched in the year 2005 to 
supplement the e fforts of the States in addressing the health care needs of underserved rural 
population by providing accessible, affordable and quality health care to them. The Mission 
adopted a health systems approach rather than vertical programmes to strengthen primar y health 
care including referrals upto District Hospital level. NRHM covered the key elements of health 
system reform namely, financing, infrastructure and equipment, improved service delivery, HR, 
governance, and community participation. The NRHM has thus  been addressing a gap which 
has been highly variable in the states. 
2.7 Before the launch of NRHM, there were vertical programmes like RCH, UIP, TB Control 
programmes, Malaria Control Programme, Blindness Control Programme etc. with specified 
targets. However it was realised and broadly acknowledged globally that vertical programmes 
cannot progress beyond a point unless backed by health systems strengthening. The health 
systems approach was also needed to address overall healthcare needs of the population.  It was 
thus decided to launch NRHM with a view to strengthen primary health care including referrals 

upto district Hospital level using health systems approach with focus on RCH and certain 
communicable diseases like TB and Malaria. 
2.8 With the approval of NHM with National Urban Health Mission and existing NRHM as 
its two Sub-Missions, the NHM has continued a health systems approach to strengthen primary 
care, including referral to District Hospitals, on the basis of global evidence that investments in 
primary health care can improve health & development outcomes at much lower cost. The 12 th 
plan aims to move towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC), which essentially requires a 
health system approach rather than vertical programmatic approach. This is als o borne out of 
global evidence from all the countries that have provided significant Universal Health 
Coverage.

II. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS 
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.7) 
3.1 The Committee notes that as compared to Rs. 21912.00 crore provided in BE 2014 -15, 
the allocation of Rs. 18,295.00 crore in BE 2015 -16 is steeply lower and is onl y marginally 
higher than the RE 2014 -15 allocation of Rs. 17627.82 crore. This small increase of Rs. 667.18 
crore in BE 2015 -16 over RE of 2014 -15 is grossly inadequate as it will be eaten up by 
inflation. The country has a huge burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases and 
studies have shown that a long and expensive illness can drive not only the non -poor into 
poverty but creates immense stress even among those who are financially secure. As is evident 
from the information furnished by the Mini stry, there is 20 percent shortfall in Sub -Centers, 23 
per cent in PHCs and 32 percent in CHCs against the norms set by Indian Public Health 
Standards (IPHS) and additional resources are required to meet this shortfall in health facilities. 
The Committee also takes note of the submissions that except for some of the advanced States, 
most of the States including the North East States are not able to augment their spending on 
health.  Keeping in view all the above facts, the Committee is extremely disappointe d with the 
low level of budgetary allocation for NHM for the financial year 2015 -16.  At the behest of the 
Committee, the Ministry has furnished two lists of activities i.e. (i) Essential activities which 
must be protected from budgetary cuts and (ii) Desi rable activities where the increase in funds 
can be made if resources are available.  The Ministry has also indicated that in order to 
undertake the essential activities, the minimum increase in allocation would be Rs. 10,500.00 
crore and thus the total BE  for 2015-16 should be Rs. 28,295.00 crore.   Keeping in view the 
fact that the Central Government has a dominance in the domain of public resource mobilization 
by way of collection of tax revenue and several States including North Eastern States will be i n 
severe handicap because of the manner in which these budgetary cuts have taken place, the 
Committee lends its full support to the demand for additional funds to the tune of Rs. 10,500. 00 
crore for undertaking the “essential activities” viz. (i) Free Dru gs and Diagnostics (ii) 
Strengthening of District Hospitals particularly in High Priority Districts and (iii) Strengthening 
of Sub Health Centres as “first port of call” to provide primary care and recommends that above 

essential activities must be protect ed from the budgetary cuts. The Committee would like the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare to immediately bring the above recommendation to 
the notice of Ministry of Finance and also intimate it of their response.  
Action Taken

DOTs would be worked out after application of due diligence and wide consultation with

recommendations contained in the 82nd Report.  They have been categorized as follows: 
 
(i)    Recommenda tions/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have been 
accepted by the Committee:  1.4, 6.3, 8.3  
                                                                                                    Total    –  3                (Chapter I)                                                          
 
(ii)   Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of 
the Government‟s replies:  7.3, 9.3, 10.2,  
                                                                                                     Total    – 3   (Chapter II)                                                                                                                                                                            
(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have 
not been accepted by the Committee:    3.5,  4.3, 5.3,  
                                                                                                    Total –       3             (Chapter III)                   
                                                                                                                                                                                  
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are 
still  awaited:     Nil                                                     Total -      Nil             (Chapter-IV) 
 
 
3. The details of the ATNs are discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH 
REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
COMMITTEE 
 
I. National Aids Control Organisation 
Recommendation/Observation (Para 1.4) 
1.1 The Committee notes that there is a declining trend of peo ple living with 
HIV/AIDS in the country according to HIV Sentinel Surveillance (HSS). The 
Committee though appreciates the efforts made by NACO  for bringing a steady 
decline in HIV prevalence in the country but would also like to know whether the 
mechanism  put in a place to count the people living with HIV/AIDS  is robust  and 
reflects the exact count.  
Action Taken 
1.2 NACO does HIV burden estimation through tools and methods recommended 
by Global reference group on HIV Estimations adapted and customized in context of 
Indian epidemic. HIV estimations 2012 made use of most comprehensive set of 
epidemiological tools and demographic data inputs available through the latest round 
of HIV Sentinel Surveillance, India Census 2011 and other data sets like that of  
National Family Health Survey. The results are assessed for validity and 
acceptability by a technical resource group of experts including representatives from 
WHO, UNAIDS etc. The mechanism put in place to estimate the HIV burden in 
country is robust and gives a reliable estimate. 
VI. Metro Blood Banks 
Recommendation/Observation (Para 6.3) 
1.3 The Committee notes that the proposal for setting up of Metro Blood Banks is 
one of the approved activities under NACP-III and has been continued in NACP-IV.  
But it s implementation is still a far cry.  Budgetary allocations to the tune of Rs. 
83.00 crore was made in BE 2014 -15 but was surrendered in toto due to pending 
approval of Expenditure Finance Committee. The Committee disapproves of 
providing as much as Rs. 83.00 crore in BE 2014-15 although  necessary approval of 
EFC remained to be obtained for implementing the project and exhorts that 

maximum possible care be taken while formulating  Budget Estimates under this 
head in future so that realistic projection of f unds requirements is ensured. Now that 
the project has been approved, the Committee recommends the Department to ensure 
that this important project is taken up for implementation without further delay.  The 
Committee would like to be updated on the progres s made towards implementation 
of this project and targeted time line for its completion.  
Action Taken  
1.4 EFC for the Metro Blood Bank Centre of Excellence project. Approval for 
initially setting up two such centres in Delhi and Chennai has been recently  granted 
by Hon‟ble HFM for an outlay of Rs 404 Crores.  
The project is to be implemented over 7 years, with the first eighteen months for 
setting up and five years of operations. The estimated start date is 1st July 2015. 
 
VIII. Antiretoviral Therapy (ART) Centre  
Recommendation/Observation (Para 8.3) 
1.5 The Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in respect of 
setting up of 134 ART centres which are proposed to be made functional by March, 
2017, within a period of six months from the date of presentation of this Report.  
Action Taken 
1.6 The progress made in respect of setting ART centers and plan for setting 
remaining ART centers by March, 17 is as follows:-

 For remaining 125 Centers plan till March, 17 is:-

CHAPTER- II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S 
REPLIES 
VII. Setting up of new District level Blood Banks 
Recommendation/Observation (Para 7.3) 
2.1 The Committee notes that the NACP -III was to be implemented during 2007 -
2012. The Committee finds that out of the 39 new District Level Blood Banks to be 
set up during NACP-III, 8 DLLB are still to be implemented even though three years 
have elapsed since NACP -III concluded.  The Committee notes that most of the 
reasons cited for the delay are non -availability of necessary infrastructure, 
manpower and delay in issuance of license. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Department to play a pro -active role by taking up the matter with the concern ed 
State Governments as well as its agencies at an appropriate level to iron out the 
procedural hindrances and help achieve the targets set.  The Committee also gathers 
that equipment for the Centres were procured and supplied during NACP -II. The 
Committee is perturbed to find such a national waste in a resource constrainted 
country like ours.  
Action Taken 
2.2 Public Health being a state subject, setting up and licensing of blood banks 
comes under purview of the respective state governments.  The Department is taking 
steps through the state governments and support of National Health Mission to set 
up atleast one blood bank in every district. There are at present 76 districts in the 
country, many of which are carved out of existing districts where there are no blood 
banks. Government is setting up blood storage centres in such districts, wherein 
existing equipments are being made use of and also providing linkage to existing 
blood banks in neighbouring districts till such time as blood banks become 
functional. The matter is being reviewed periodically at both state and national level.   
 
IX. Setting up of Plasma Fractionation Centre (PFC)  
Recommendation/Observation (Para 9.3) 

2.3 The Committee desires that the project should take off at the earliest.  All 
necessary steps may be taken in this direction.  
 
Action  Taken 
2.4 As an immediate measure for arrangements for plasma fractionation, the 
department is finalizing an exchange value for plasma to be provided to indigenous 
fractionators of India, while paralle lly deliberating a strategy for Public Private 
partnership through a special purpose vehicle. It is also pertinent to mention here 
that for the fractionation centre to be viable, it requires a surplus of 1.5 lakh litres of 
plasma, which is presently not be ing separated across blood banks in the country. 
Efforts are also being focused by the department for improving the separation of 
components and generation of adequate volume of plasma. 
 
X. Setting up of District AIDS Prevention and Control Units (DAPCUs)  
Recommendation/Observation (Para 10.2) 
2.5 The Committee appreciates the efforts of NACO to set up 189 DAPCUs in the 
country. The Committee notes that further expansion of DAPCUs would be 
undertaken, if required, after finalization of district re-categorization which is still in 
process. The Committee recommends that the district re-categorization should be 
completed at the earliest.  
  
Action Taken 
2.6 The district re -categorization process had been initiated as a follow up to the exercise of 
„District Epidemiological Profiling Using Data Triangulation‟ during 2012 -13.  So, after review of 
draft report of district re -categorization process in NACO, it has been decided to update the 
framework for re -categorization of districts with latest HIV Sentinel Surve illance (HSS 2014 -15) 
reports data and National Integrated Bio -Behavioral Surveillance (IBBS) reports data. These 
reports are expected in few months. 
2.7 Based on the updated data, district re-categorization process implementation 
plan would be worked out after finalisation of the same. 
 

 
 
CHAPTER - III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH 
REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE COMMITTEE 
II. Budgetary Allocation 
Recommendation/Observation (Para 3.5) 
3.1 The Committee notes that as compared to the funds allotted in REs 2012 -13, 
2013-14 and 2014 -15, the level of utilization of funds by NACO has been 
satisfactory, though it is less than the allocations made in BEs of the respective 
years.  A perusal of the information made available  to the Committee, revealed that 
according to HIV Sentinel Surveillance 2012 -13, which is mandated to assess the 
burden and trends of HIV in different States of the country, the overall HIV 
prevalence among the general population continues to be low at 0.3 5% in the 
country, with an overall declining trend at the national level.  The estimated number 
of People Living with HIV/AIDS has also maintained a steady declining trend from 
23.2 lakh in 2006 to 20.9 lakh in 2011.  The Committee feels that this is due t o the 
impact of the various interventions of NACP and scaled up prevention strategies.  
But what is worrisome is that some low prevalence States like Assam, Chandigarh, 
Delhi, Jharkhand etc. have shown increase in the number of new infections. In this 
context the Committee is concerned about the reduced allocation for NACO for 
2015-16.  The Committee feels that the allocation of Rs.1397.00 crore in BE 2015 -
16  which is only marginally higher than the RE 2014 -15 allocation of Rs.1300.00 
crore may have an adv erse impact on the key priorities of National AIDS Control 
Programme IV and hinder scale-up  of interventions in hitherto untouched areas. The 
Committee sincerely hopes that subsequent to the increase of State share in the 
Central Taxes from 32 per cent to  42 per cent, the State Governments, who are 
currently not contributing any money to National AIDS Control Programme 
(NACP), would be able to fund a proportion of the fund requirement from their State 
Health Budgets. The Committee, simultaneously, observes  that India is a resource -
constrained country and in order to obtain the best possible health outcomes, it is 

imperative that allocation of resources is prioritized across competing ends and the 
available funds are deployed in a more efficient manner.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that concrete steps should be initiated to economize on expenditure and 
improve its efficiency so that the intended objectives of NACP IV are not adversely 
impacted.   
 
Action Taken 
3.2      Views of the Committee over the decline in HIV prevalence in country, 
number of Peoples living with HIV/AIDS (PLIHV) and satisfactory use of allotted 
funds by NACO are acknowledged with gratitude. The concern of the Committee 
over the increase in the number of new infections in some low prevalence States and 
apprehension of suffering of the programme due to allocation of Rs. 1397.00 crore 
only in BE 2015-16, a little higher than RE 2014-15 of Rs. 1300.00 crore cannot also 
be ruled out. To have sufficient funds for the programme the matter  for contribution 
from States has already been taken up at different levels. The need of strict 
prioritization and effective, efficient and economical use of resources are also 
reminded to all concerned from time to time to have best use of the resources o f the 
country. 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.3 While making its recommendation in para 3.5  of Part C of its 82 nd 
Report, the Committee had hoped that with the increase of State share in 
Central taxes from 32% to 42%, the States would be able  to fund a propor tion 
of the fund requirement for AIDS Control Programmes from their State Health 
Budgets.  The Committee, however, notes with concern that instead of making 
any empirical study  to determine the impact of the new Centre -State  tax 
sharing model on States' expenditures on the AIDS Control Programmes, the 
NACO  has given a generic and routine reply, stating that "  To have sufficient 
funds for the programme the matter for contribution from States has already 
been taken up at different levels".  The Committee, therefore, recommends that 

the NACO  should conduct an evaluatory  study in the right earnest on whether 
all the States have the additional fiscal space for allocating resources for the 
AIDS Control programmes and whether the States have budgeted any funds  
for the AIDS Control Programmes in their Budgets for the financial year 2015 -
16. 
IV Unspent Cash Balances with State AIDS Control Society (SACS)  
Recommendation/Observation (Para 4.3) 
3.4 The Committee notes that in spite of interventions of NACO, availab ility of 
unspent balances with some SACS are still quite high. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the NACO to introduce stricter monitoring mechanism and plan viable 
strategy to clear the unspent balances so that funds do not get accumulated and 
locked but are utilized in a more productive manner.  The Committee also reiterates 
its earlier recommendation made in its 70 th Report on Demands for Grants 2013 -14 
of the erstwhile Department of AIDS Control that in order to ensure timely and 
effective utilization of unspent balances, NACO should insist on quarterly feedback 
from all the SACS. The Committee also desires to be apprised of the number and 
dates of review meetings taken in 2014 -15 to expedite liquidation of the unspent 
cash balances with SACS.   
 
Action Taken 
3.5  The views of the Committee w.r.t. need of adopting further strict  measures to 
minimize the unspent balance in respect of some SACS are welcome and remedial 
measures, interalia the quarterly monitoring of the unspent cash balance, will be 
taken.   During the year 2014 -15, review meetings were taken in the month of July, 
2014, January 2015 and March 2015. There are constant efforts to liquidate the 
unspent balance to minimum, but certain balances say up to 15 -20 % of release are 
genuinely required to carry on affairs during the time gap of the recommendation of 
the release and actual transfer of the funds to the SACS by the treasury. 

3.6 It may not be out of place to mention that the instances of the delay in transfer 
of money to SACS by the treasuries have been noticed and are being addressed at 
different levels. 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.7   The Committee feels concerned to note that the treasury route of transfer 
of funds has led to delay  in transfer of money to SACS.  The Committee feels 
that if this trend is allowed to persist, it will certainly drag down the level of 
utilisation of budgeted funds, thereby impacting the intended outcomes on the 
one hand and resulting in surrender of the scarce resources on the other.   In 
this context, the C ommittee would suggest that the issue of mode of transfer of 
funds should be taken up with the Ministry of Finance on an urgent basis so 
that the time lag in release of funds to the State AIDS Control Societies is 
reduced.  The Committee is certain that in  this age of information technology, 
this would not be an insurmountable task.   
V. Role  of NGOs 
Recommendation/Observation (Para 5.3) 
3.8 The Committee welcomes the action initiated by NACO to deal with the 
issues - like recovery of unspent balances with  discontinued NGOs and steps taken 
for monitoring and control of programmatic and financial activities etc. The 
Committee would, however, like the Department to make an assessment of the 
impact of actions initiated for a recovery of unspent balances with d efaulting 
NGO‟s.  
Action Taken 
3.9 National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) has initiated number of 
mechanisms against defaulting NGOs implementing Targeted Intervention 
Programme and the impact seen by NACO of the actions initiated for a recovery of 
unspent balances with defaulting NGOs is that the outstanding amount against the 
defaulting NGOS to be recovered has declined from Rs 352.17 lakhs to 73.33 lakhs 
and a follow-up plan is developed to monitor the recovery of unspent balances with 

defaulting NGOs with States AIDS Control Society (SACS) on a monthly basis. If 
the amount is not recovered even after legal notices, SACS have started 
communicating to Planning and Coordination Department, for blacklisting the 
NGOs and involving District Collectors to recover the balance amount.  
 
Further Recommendation 
3.10 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department with 
regard to the defaulting NGOs due to which the outstanding amount has 
declined from Rs.352.00 lakhs to 73.33 lakhs. The Committee note s that States 
AIDS Control Societies (SACS) have started communicating to Planning and 
Coordination Department and District Collectors to recover the balance 
amount from blacklisted NGOs. The Committee would like to be informed of 
the efficacy of the measu res taken on the recovery of balances from defaulting 
NGOs.

AYUSH
I.         INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy which was set up by the Government of India
as an independent department in March, 1995, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare was renamed as
Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) in November, 2003.   The
main objective of the Department is to provide focused attention for the proper development and propagation of
Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and to fully utilize the potentials of these systems.
1.2       Thrust areas of the Department are: -
i)
                    Improvement and up-gradation of standards of education in AYUSH;
ii)                   Quality Control and Standardization of drugs;
iii)                 Ensuring sustained availability of raw materials, i.e. medicinal plants, metals, minerals and materials of
animal origin etc;
iv)                 Research & Development on the efficacy of the systems;
v)                  Participation of AYUSH in the National Health Care Delivery System & National Health & Family Welfare
Programme;
vi)                 Information, Education and Communication.
 
1.3       Over the years, there has been a steady growth in infrastructure of AYUSH.   At present, number of practitioners
of AYUSH in the country is 6,95,024.   There are 549 teaching institutions which include 454 Undergraduate colleges
and 95 Post-Graduate colleges.   Number of drug manufacturing units both in Govt. and private sector in the country is
9257.    There are 3100 Hospitals and 20811 dispensaries in the Govt. sector out of which maximum number of
hospitals and dispensaries provide Ayurvedic system of treatment.  Total number of Ayurveda Hospitals in the country
are 2253 and number of dispensaries in the                  country is 13925.
 
1.4       The Secretary, during the course of her presentation before the Committee, stated that the Department received
actual visibility during the Tenth Plan with the introduction of a number of Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored
Schemes aimed at development of educational institutions, research and quality control, hospitals and dispensaries etc. 
Achievements made during the year 2004-05 included establishment of ISMH wings in 23 district hospitals, 8 speciality
clinics/polyclinics, supply of essential drugs to 8152 AYUSH dispensaries in rural and backward areas, improvement of
educational infrastructure in respect of 120 educational institutions of AYUSH in the country. The Committee was also
informed that the only public sector undertaking of the Department i.e. the Indian Medicines Pharmaceutical
Corporation Limited (IMPCL), Mohan, Uttaranchal enhanced its turnover from about Rs. 3.35 crores in 2002-03 to Rs.
6.00 crores in 2004-05.   The Secretary pointed out that as a result of various activities undertaken during the year,
entire plan allocation of Rs. 200.00 crores for the year 2004-05 was utilised.

II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
2.1       The Plan Allocation of the Department for the year 2005-06 is Rs. 350.00 crore including Rs. 5.00 crore for the
Department of Urban Development for the completion of building for Pharmacopoeial Laboratory of Indian Medicine
(PLIM) and Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeial Laboratory (HPL).   Non-Plan allocation of the Department for 2005-06 is
Rs. 60.98 crore.  Whereas Plan allocation for 2005-06 has been substantially enhanced when compared with RE 2004-
05 allocation of   Rs. 200 crores, non-Plan allocation for 2005-06 does not reflect any increase. 
 
2.2       The Committee was informed that during the first two years of Tenth Plan, allocation of Rs. 150 crores in each
year remained underutilized due to various reasons.  The two main reasons were delay in approval of some centrally
sponsored schemes and lack of awareness among the implementing agencies about the schemes.  The Plan allocation of
the Department during the year 2004-05 was Rs.173.00 crore (excluding Rs. 8.00 crore for the Department of Urban
Development). Considering the performance of the Department and increased requirements of funds to implement
various Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  BE allocation was raised to Rs. 200.00 crore at RE Stage.  
Expenditure reported upto 28
th March, 2005 is Rs. 195.26 crore.  
 
2.3       The Committee was given to understand that an enhanced provision has been made  for 2005-06, in view of
genuine requirements of the Department under the various on-going programmes and its capacity  to utilize the
proposed provisions.   
The Department was confident of spending the increased budget provisions in 2005-06 as the Centrally Sponsored
Schemes under implementation are fully subscribed.  The Department was rather facing paucity of budget provisions in
implementing even feasible proposals under some of the schemes.
 
2.4       The Committee notes that against an allocation of Rs. 364.43 crore during the Ninth Plan, funds amounting to
only Rs. 293.72 crore could be utilised.   An enhanced allocation of Rs. 775 crore has been made for the Tenth Plan. 
The Committee notes that although utilisation position of allocated funds in the first year of the Tenth Plan i.e. 2002-03
was not satisfactory,  during the  second year,  the Department could utilise the entire allocation provided at the RE
stage.   For 2004-05, provision of Rs. 173 crore was enhanced to Rs. 200 crore.   The Department justified this enhanced
allocation by utilizing Rs. 195.26 crore by 28
th March, 2005. 
 
2.5       The Committee notes with satisfaction that with the increase in allocation, capacity of the Department to utilise
the same is also increasing.  The Committee would, however, like to point out that trend of utilisation is not evenly
spread in all the quarters of the financial year of 2004-05.   Against plan allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore in 2004-05, the
Department could utilise Rs. 121.33 crore  by the end of third quarter, i.e. 31st December, 2005.  By 7th March, 2005   it
increased to Rs. 179.49 crore and by the 28 th March, 05, utilisation figures were Rs. 195.26 crore.   This clearly shows
that out of total allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore in 2004-05, an expenditure of RS. 74.00 crore was made in the last

3.3       In contrast, in the case of CCIM, there has been optimum utilisation of  allocated funds varying from Rs. 10 to

allergy etc. The Committee welcomes this ambitious partnership programme and hopes that research work to be
undertaken under this project will yield fruitful results for all concerned.

OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
            The Committee notes that against an allocation of Rs. 364.43 crore during the Ninth Plan, funds amounting to
only Rs. 293.72 crore could be utilised.   An enhanced allocation of Rs. 775 crore has been made for the Tenth Plan. 
The Committee notes that although utilisation position of allocated funds in the first year of the Tenth Plan i.e. 2002-03
was not satisfactory, during the second year, the Department could utilise the entire allocation provided at the RE
stage.   For 2004-05, provision of Rs. 173 crore was enhanced to Rs. 200 crore.   The Department justified this enhanced
allocation by utilizing Rs. 195.26 crore by 28
th March, 2005.  (Para 2.4)
 
            The Committee notes with satisfaction that with the increase in allocation, capacity of the Department to utilise
the same is also increasing.  The Committee would, however, like to point out that trend of utilisation is not evenly
spread in all the quarters of the financial year of 2004-05.   Against plan allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore in 2004-05, the
Department could utilise Rs. 121.33 crore  by the end of third quarter, i.e. 31
st December, 2005.  By 7th March, 2005   it
increased to Rs. 179.49 crore and by the 28 th March, 05, utilisation figures were Rs. 195.26 crore.   This clearly shows
that out of total allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore in 2004-05, an expenditure of RS. 74.00 crore was made in the last
quarter of the year.  The Committee is of the view that the pace of utilisation should be as per the prescribed financial
norms.   Expenditure on the high side in the last quarter of the financial year cannot be considered good for the health of
budget planning. (Para 2.5) 
 
2.7       The Committee, accordingly, requests that the Department should make concerted efforts for optimum and

judicious utilisation of allocated funds in individual schemes/programmes to the extent possible. (Para 2.7) 
 
III STATUTORY INSTITUTIONS
 
             The Committee would like to be enlightened in this regard.  Committee’s attention has also been drawn by
provision of Rs. 20 lakhs in 2003-04 for conducting elections of CCH which remained unutilized due to the fact that
elections could not be conducted.  Provision was there for this purpose in 2002-03 also.  These elections seem to have
been finally conducted during the year 2004-05 as the provision meant for this purpose has been utilised.  The
Committee would like to know as to whether both these statutory bodies are duly constituted with full membership.
(Para 3.4) 
 
   The Committee, however, finds that in the case of CCIM, during 2004-05, Central Register of Delhi and Tamil Nadu
was updated upto March, 2001 and in the case of Orissa and Rajasthan upto March, 2002.   The Committee fails to
understand the factors responsible for the Central Register of Indian Medicine not being updated.   The Committee
would like to be apprised about the position in respect of other States.  The Committee would also like to have an idea
about the status of the Central Register being maintained by the Central Council of Homoeopathy. (Para 3.5) 
 
        The Committee is of the view that there needs to be an effective monitoring mechanism for regulating the AYUSH
doctors practising across the country.The Committee, therefore, recommends that immediate action is required to be
taken either by the two councils or any other body which is empowered to regulate in such matters. (Para 3.6) 
 
IV.       CENTRAL PHARMACY COUNCIL FOR AYUSH
The Committee is constrained to observe that during 2004-05 also, position remained the same.  The Committee
finds that during 2005-06 Rs. 1 crore has been provided for the proposed Council.  The Department has informed that
the Bill has been prepared and the comments of the Ministries of Finance, HRD and Health & Family Welfare
obtained.   The draft Bill is almost ready and will be introduced in Parliament shortly.  The Committee reiterates that
there should be no further delay for introducing the Bill in Parliament.    (Para 4.1) 
 
V. HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
Advanced Ayurvedic Centre  for Mental Health in NIMHANS
The Committee observes that although Rs. 97 lakhs were spent during the Ninth Plan period, nothing seems to
have materialized in the operationalisation of the centre.  The Committee has to make such a comment only because of
trend of expenditure in the three years of the Tenth Plan.  Rs. 26 lakhs were provided in 2002-03 but the allocated funds
remained unutilized.    There was no provision during 2003-04.  However, in 2004-05 Rs. 1 lakh has been provided for
this Centre.  The Committee strongly feels that any scheme/plan proposed to be implemented should only be taken up
after due consideration of its feasibility and other allied aspects.  Advanced Ayurvedic Centre for Mental Health in
NIMHANS, Bangalore seems to have been forsaken by the Department.  The Committee would like to be apprised
about the actual status of this Centre.   (Para 5.1)  
 
VI.       RESEARCH COUNCILS (INTRA & EXTRA ) MURAL RESEARCH
            The Committee observes that during 2004-05 physical targets could not be achieved fully inspite of there being
full utilisation of funds.  Plan allocation for 2005-06 stands at Rs. 12.50 crore which is higher than Rs. 8 crore provided
in 2004-05.  The Committee would like to emphasize that all required steps should be taken for achieving the physical
targets for which plan funds are meant for.  The Committee observed that during the last two years of Ninth Plan also
physical targets could not be achieved fully.  The Committee apprehends that during the Tenth Plan also, so far, the
position may be the same.  If that be so, then there is a need for making quarterly assessment about the achievement of
physical targets.  (Para 6.2)  
 
VII.     CENTRAL COUNCIL FOR RESEARCH INSTITUTE OF UNANI MEDICINE, NEW DELHI
The Committee would like to be apprised about the specific purpose for which this additional allocation is meant
for.  The Committee would also like to point out that the construction of building for RRUM has been continuing for

The Committee would like to have an idea of quantum of funds spent on construction activities during the first
three years of Tenth Plan.  The Committee would also like to know about the status of all the research Institutes
